evidence.title: Kapova Cave (Shulgan-Tash, Southern Urals): ~18 ka Paleolithic Red-Ochre Murals
evidence.dateBasis: U-series calcite & radiocarbon hearth dates
evidence.summary: Deep limestone caverns in Bashkortostan preserve painted wooly mammoths, horses, rhinoceroses, and geometric signs crafted by Upper Paleolithic Uralian foragers.
evidence.limits: Pigment panels experienced calcite flowstone growth over multiple LGM visits.

evidence.title: Shamanka II & Lokomotiv (Lake Baikal): Early Holocene Kitoi–Glazkovo Cemeteries
evidence.dateBasis: AMS bone collagen & ancient genomes
evidence.summary: Stratified Lake Baikal hunter-fisher necropolises document Kitoi red-ochre burials, composite fishhooks, nephrite rings, and Yeniseian-related ancestral turnovers.
evidence.limits: Reservoir corrections affect freshwater-fish diets in Cis-Baikal radiocarbon ages.

evidence.title: Kovrizhka IV & Tunka Rift Valleys (East Siberia): Late Glacial Ochre Hearths
evidence.dateBasis: Stratified alluvial radiocarbon & OSGL
evidence.summary: Microblade hearths dusted with ground hematite along the Vitim and Tunka Valleys trace subarctic mobility between Baikal and the Patom Highlands.
evidence.limits: Seasonal alluvial floods cap thin occupation lenses.

evidence.title: Chernoozerye II & Bolshoye Bakalskoye (Irtysh–Tobol): Baraba–Sargat Horse Lords
evidence.dateBasis: Stratigraphy, pottery typology & radiocarbon
evidence.summary: From Late Paleolithic horse-bone hunting stations to Iron Age Sargat elite kurgans along the Middle Irtysh, forest-steppe communities bridged Siberian taiga furs with southern Silk oases.
evidence.limits: Ploughing and riverbank erosion have truncated outer ditch earthworks.

evidence.title: Great Salbyk Kurgan (Minusinsk Basin, Khakassia): Monumental Tagar Sandstone Sanctuary
evidence.dateBasis: Dendrochronology & Iron Age typology
evidence.summary: Thirty-ton upright Devonian sandstone slabs imported 70 km enclose a massive Tagar Scythian-horizon royal pyramid anchoring Minusinsk bronze metallurgy and pastoral authority.
evidence.limits: Ancient looting disturbed inner wooden burial chambers before modern excavation.

evidence.title: Bashadar & Tuekta Frozen Barrows (Ursul Valley, Altai): Permafrost Timber & Horse Regalia
evidence.dateBasis: Tree-ring wiggle-matching & Pazyryk textiles
evidence.summary: Ice lenses preserved cedar-log sarcophagi engraved with snow leopards, felt saddle covers, imported Achaemenid woolens, and harnessed sacrificial steppe horses.
evidence.limits: Warming mountain permafrost threatens remaining unexcavated Altai ice barrows.

evidence.title: Ust-Yodarma II (Northern Angara, Irkutsk): Multilayered Taiga Geoarchaeological Sequence
evidence.dateBasis: Alluvial stratigraphy & lithic-ceramic seriation
evidence.summary: Twenty-two superimposed cultural horizons along the Northern Angara trace uninterrupted Holocene boreal hunting, net-fishing, and bronze-casting adaptation.
evidence.limits: Rescue excavations preceded filling of the Boguchany Reservoir basin.

evidence.title: Gasya & Khummi Stratified Camps (Lower Amur, Khabarovsk): Ice Age Amur River Pottery
evidence.dateBasis: Organic temper AMS & TL dating
evidence.summary: Coarse fiber-tempered flat-bottomed cooking vessels paired with laurel-leaf bifaces confirm independent salmon-harvesting ceramic innovation along the Amur before farming.
evidence.limits: Acidic boreal soils limit organic bone recovery.

evidence.title: Boisman II & Yankovsky Shell Middens (Peter the Great Bay, Primorye): Maritime Pacific Cultures
evidence.dateBasis: Marine-shell calibrated C14 & osteology
evidence.summary: Coastal Primorye cemeteries and thick oyster middens reveal marine mammal toggling harpoons, composite bows, and Early Iron Age millet-sea exchange with the Korean Peninsula.
evidence.limits: Coastal transgression submerged earlier Pleistocene shorelines in the Sea of Japan.

evidence.title: Tarasovsky & Gladenovsky Bone Sanctuaries (Kama Basin, Cis-Urals): Perm Finno-Ugric Worlds
evidence.dateBasis: Grave goods, Sasanian silver & radiocarbon
evidence.summary: More than 1,800 Iron Age burials and sacrificial bone mounds in the Kama riverlands linked Uralic-speaking trappers with Sasanian Persian silver dishes traded northward for sable pelts.
evidence.limits: Acidic podzol preserves iron, silver, and cremated fragments better than textiles.

evidence.title: Staraya Ladoga (Volkhov River, NW Russia): 753 CE Fur-Silver Emporium
evidence.dateBasis: Dendrochronology of oak & pine log structures
evidence.summary: Tree-ring dated wooden workshops and Baltic-to-Volga Abbasid dirham hoards mark Staraya Ladoga as a founding trans-Eurasian river-port linking Scandinavia, Rus principalities, and Central Asia.
evidence.limits: Timber waterlogging ceases above the medieval cultural layer.

evidence.title: Veliky Novgorod (Detinets & Nerevsky Quarter): Birch-Bark Literacy & Guild Republic
evidence.dateBasis: Dendrochronology & >1,100 birch-bark manuscripts
evidence.summary: Timber-paved streets and ordinary citizens' birch-bark letters (*beresty*) document Novgorod's merchant assembly (*veche*) and Arctic fur-tribute networks reaching from Karelia to the Ob River.
evidence.limits: Anaerobic wet clay protects birch bark only within low-lying medieval quarters.

evidence.title: Vladimir & Suzdal White-Stone Monasteries (Opolye Plain): Medieval Rus Civic Architecture
evidence.dateBasis: Architectural stratigraphy & chronicle inscriptions
evidence.summary: Limestone-carved Assumption Cathedral, Pokrov-on-the-Nerl, and Suzdal Kremlin monasteries anchor the northeastward political and artistic shift of Rus toward the upper Volga.
evidence.limits: Repeated restorations followed 13th-century Mongol sieges.

evidence.title: Moscow Kremlin, Zaryadye & Kitay-Gorod: Muscovite Synthesis & Imperial Statecraft
evidence.dateBasis: Excavated oak ramparts, brick walls & diplomatic archives
evidence.summary: Excavations in Zaryadye and the Kremlin uncover Moscow's rise from a Moskva River wooden fort into an imperial capital blending Orthodox liturgy, Italian Renaissance brickwork, and Eurasian caravan diplomacy.
evidence.limits: Dense modern construction restricts open-area excavation inside the Kremlin walls.

evidence.title: Ancient Bolgar (Volga–Kama Confluence, Tatarstan): 10th–15th c. Steppe-Forest Metropolis
evidence.dateBasis: Coin hoards, cast-iron foundries & stone mosques
evidence.summary: Volga Bulgaria's stone bathhouses, White Chamber, and cast-iron workshops served as both an early Muslim center visited by Ibn Fadlan and the northern commercial capital of the Golden Horde.
evidence.limits: Kuibyshev Reservoir flooded lower Volga riverine docks.

evidence.title: Kazan Kremlin & Old Tatar Quarter (Middle Volga): Khanate-to-Eurasian Crossroads
evidence.dateBasis: Stratified khanate masonry, charters & mosque/cathedral fabric
evidence.summary: Söyembikä Tower, the Annunciation Cathedral, and Old Tatar Quarter preserve six centuries of Volga Tatar Islamic scholarship and Russian imperial synthesis at the hinge of the Volga route to Siberia.
evidence.limits: 1552 siege layers were overlaid by Muscovite limestone bastions.

evidence.title: Nizhny Novgorod Kremlin & Makaryev Fair (Volga–Oka Confluence): Eurasian Guild Market
evidence.dateBasis: Customs ledgers & Kremlin masonry
evidence.summary: Positioned where the Oka meets the Volga, Nizhny Novgorod's fair channeled Ural iron, Chinese tea, Bukharan cotton, and Siberian pelts across Eurasian waterways.
evidence.limits: Wooden seasonal bazaar pavilions left fewer remains than brick fair halls.

evidence.title: Astrakhan Citadel & Volga Delta Entrepôt (Lower Volga): Caspian Silk–Salt Gateway
evidence.dateBasis: White-stone kremlin masonry & caravanserai records
evidence.summary: Commanding the Caspian mouth of the Volga, Astrakhan's Russian, Persian, Indian, and Armenian merchant yards linked South Asia and Safavid Iran with Muscovy.
evidence.limits: Earlier Golden Horde Xacitarxan lies eroded upstream of the modern citadel.

evidence.title: Solovetsky Monastery Fortress (White Sea Archipelago): Arctic Salt, Fisheries & Heritage
evidence.dateBasis: Boulder walls, salt-boiling pans & monastic chronicles
evidence.summary: Granite boulder fortifications and canal-linked glacial lakes anchored northern Russian monastic literacy, salt evaporation, and Pomor maritime navigation across the White and Barents Seas.
evidence.limits: 20th-century penal alterations overlay several outer skete buildings.

evidence.title: Cherdyn, Solikamsk & Usolye Stroganov Estates (Upper Kama, Perm): Salt-to-Siberia Launchpad
evidence.dateBasis: Salt-brine towers, stone churches & Stroganov ledgers
evidence.summary: Great Perm saltworks financed the Stroganov workshops, illuminated liturgical icons, and early Ural crossings that launched Muscovite river expeditions into western Siberia.
evidence.limits: Flooding along the Kama Reservoir inundated lower brine derricks.

evidence.title: Verkhoturye Kremlin & Babinov Road (Central Urals): Imperial Customs Gate to Siberia
evidence.dateBasis: Toll registers, kremlin brick & St. Nicholas Monastery
evidence.summary: For over a century after 1598, every caravan and migrant bound for Siberia passed through Verkhoturye's customs barrier on the Tura River along the shortened Babinov Trail.
evidence.limits: 18th-century bypass highways reduced toll traffic after 1763.

evidence.title: Tyumen (1586) & Tara (1594) Fortress Towns (Tura–Irtysh): First Urban Grid in Siberia
evidence.dateBasis: Ostrog timber foundations, ceramics & Tobol-Ishim surveys
evidence.summary: Founded immediately east of the Urals alongside Bukharan merchant quarters (*Bukharlyk*), Tyumen and Tara fused Russian timber forts with Siberian Tatar and Central Asian caravan neighborhoods.
evidence.limits: Subsurface moisture shifts alter wooden palisade preservation.

evidence.title: Tomsk Ostrog & White-Stone Resurrection Quarter (Tom River): Ob–Chulym Crossroads
evidence.dateBasis: Kremlin hilltop trenches & wooden merchant lacework
evidence.summary: Built at the request of Eushta Tatar prince Toyan in 1604, Tomsk became the main junction between West Siberian river barges and overland tracks toward Krasnoyarsk and the Yenisei.
evidence.limits: Original 1604 Voskresenskaya Hill stockade rebuilt after 17th-century fires.

evidence.title: Yeniseysk Monastery-Ostrog & Makovskoye Portage (Middle Yenisei): River Hub of 1619
evidence.dateBasis: Monastery charters & Ket-Yenisei portage archaeology
evidence.summary: Anchored across the Ket–Yenisei watershed divide, Yeniseysk equipped expeditions descending the Lower Tunguska toward the Lena, while gold-rush wealth financed distinctive Siberian baroque churches.
evidence.limits: Wooden docklands suffered periodic spring ice-jam floods.

evidence.title: Bratsk Ostrog & Ilimsk Portage (Angara–Ilim Basin): Buryat Frontier & Lena Gateway
evidence.dateBasis: Relocated 17th-century oak watchtowers & customs books
evidence.summary: Relocated watchtowers from Bratsk and Ilimsk illustrate the log-fort architecture and Lena portage logistics that tied Irkutsk to Yakutia's fur frontier.
evidence.limits: Bratsk and Ust-Ilimsk hydroelectric dams submerged original ostrogs; surviving towers were moved to museums.

evidence.title: Barnaul & Kolyvan-Voskresensk Silver Smelters (Altai Piedmont): 18th c. Imperial Mint
evidence.dateBasis: Slag heaps, Demidov furnace plans & mining censuses
evidence.summary: Demidov and imperial Cabinet smelters around Barnaul turned ancient Chud/Bronze-Age Altai polymetallic lodes into Russia's foremost 18th-century silver and stone-cutting industrial center.
evidence.limits: Early water-powered dams were replaced by 19th-century steam mills.

evidence.title: Chita Ostrog & Transbaikal Wooden Church Towns (Ingoda–Shilka): Amur-Tea Junction
evidence.dateBasis: Log church architecture & Transbaikal post registers
evidence.summary: Linking the Selenga–Baikal route with the Shilka and Amur headwaters, Chita anchored Cossack settlements, Old Believer villages, and the later Trans-Siberian junction.
evidence.limits: 18th-century timber post-stations were largely replaced by masonry after 1851.

evidence.title: Albazin (Yaksa) Fortress (Upper Amur): 1651–1689 Sino-Russian Frontier Crucible
evidence.dateBasis: Earthen rampart trenches, lead shot & bilingual treaty archives
evidence.summary: Earthen redoubts above the Amur preserve siege traces between Khabarov/Chernigovsky settlers and Kangxi's Qing bannermen that culminated in the 1689 Treaty of Nerchinsk.
evidence.limits: Abandoned and dismantled under treaty terms for nearly 170 years until 1858.

evidence.title: Nizhny Tagil & Nevyansk Leaning Tower (Middle Urals): 18th-Century Iron Frontier
evidence.dateBasis: Blast-furnace masonry, copper mines & Ural archives
evidence.summary: Water-powered blast furnaces in the Urals exported bar iron down the Chusovaya–Kama–Volga waterways to Europe while supplying anchors, bells, and rails across Siberia.
evidence.limits: 19th-century railway expansion rebuilt most original wooden dams.

evidence.title: Vladivostok Golden Horn & Nikolayevsk-on-Amur: 19th-Century Pacific Ports
evidence.dateBasis: Coastal battery masonry & Trans-Siberian terminus surveys
evidence.summary: Following the 1858–1860 Amur treaties, Vladivostok and Nikolayevsk linked East Asian sea lanes from Nagasaki and Shanghai directly to European Russia via maritime steam and transcontinental rail.
evidence.limits: Later concrete sea-forts obscured mid-19th-century timber wharves.

evidence.title: Gizhiga, Anadyr Estuary & Avacha Bay (NE Siberia): 18th–19th c. Arctic Cartography & Contact
evidence.dateBasis: Expedition cartography (Bering, Mydel) & ostrog trenches
evidence.summary: Kamchatka harbors and Chukotka tundra expeditions under Bering and later Gerhardt von Mydel mapped the Bering Strait, negotiated Chukchi–Evenki autonomy, and launched Pacific-American voyages.
evidence.limits: Tundra and volcanic seismicity erase fragile 18th-century timber posts.

evidence.title: Kizhi Pogost (Lake Onega) & Totma Baroque (Northern Waterways): Timber Craft & Fur Trade
evidence.dateBasis: Axe-hewn pine carpentry & Totma merchant cartouches
evidence.summary: Multi-domed nail-free timber churches on Lake Onega and maritime-funded Totma–Baikal baroque facades track wealth accumulated by northern Russian Arctic and Aleutian fur merchants.
evidence.limits: High-latitude timber requires continuous shingle restoration.

evidence.title: Omsk Fortress & Irtysh Cossack Line (SW Siberia): Steppe Borderland Synthesis
evidence.dateBasis: Star-bastion masonry, Lutheran–Orthodox–Mosque records
evidence.summary: Anchoring the Irtysh fortified frontier with the Kazakh Steppe, Omsk grew into West Siberia's administrative seat connecting steppe livestock caravans with Trans-Ural trade.
evidence.limits: 1716 wooden fort replaced by a brick star-fortress in 1768.

evidence.title: Tobolsk Kremlin & Sofia Cathedral (Irtysh–Tobol Confluence): Stone Heart of Old Siberia
evidence.dateBasis: Siberian chronicles, Kremlin brick masonry & archeology
evidence.summary: Erected above the confluence of the Tobol and Irtysh near the former Khanate capital of Isker, Tobolsk housed Siberia's first archbishopric, stone kremlin, cartographer Semyon Remezov, and tea customs.
evidence.limits: Hillside landslides along the Irtysh escarpment periodically threatened outer ramparts.

evidence.title: St. Petersburg Admiralty, Kunstkamera & Neva Docks: Imperial Maritime Hinge (1703–1900)
evidence.dateBasis: Imperial Academy of Sciences archives & Vyshny Volochok canal
evidence.summary: Linked directly to the Volga basin by Peter I's Vyshny Volochok canal, St. Petersburg financed the Great Northern Expeditions across Siberia and housed Asian–Pacific ethnographic collections in the Kunstkamera.
evidence.limits: Represents imperial administration rather than deep prehistoric origins.

evidence.title: Samara Bend & Ukek (Middle Volga): Golden Horde River Cities & Pastoral Crossings
evidence.dateBasis: Kilns, polychrome kashin ceramics & Volga stratigraphy
evidence.summary: Cosmopolitan Golden Horde Volga river towns such as Ukek fused steppe pastoralist elites with Russian, Italian, Persian, and Bulgar artisans before Moscow fortified Samara in 1586.
evidence.limits: Volga bank slumping continues to erode Ukek riverfront strata.

evidence.title: Qi Great Wall (Shandong Ridge to Yellow Sea): Earliest State Frontier Rampart
evidence.dateBasis: Rammed-earth & dry-stone sections; Spring & Autumn annals
evidence.summary: Stretching over 600 km across Shandong mountain passes from Pingyin to the sea, the State of Qi rampart pioneered coordinated multi-pass frontier wall engineering centuries before Qin unification.
evidence.limits: Agricultural terracing leveled lowland segments while ridge stones survive.

evidence.title: Qin–Zhao Yinshan Frontier Wall & Guyang Beacons (Inner Mongolia): 221 BCE Unification
evidence.dateBasis: Earthenware tile-end typology & Qin watchtower GIS
evidence.summary: General Meng Tian joined earlier Zhao and Qin dry-stone mountain barriers along the Yinshan arc above the Ordos bend, marking an enduring ecological boundary between millet farms and steppe pasture.
evidence.limits: Surface erosion blurs unreinforced tamped-earth sections.

evidence.title: Hexi Corridor Han Great Wall & Signal Beacons (Wuwei–Dunhuang): Linear Remote Sensing
evidence.dateBasis: Reed-and-gravel stratigraphy & high-res satellite survey
evidence.summary: Tamped layers of Gobi gravel alternating with tamarisk reeds formed an arid-adapted wall and fire-beacon telegraph sheltering caravans bound for Central Asia.
evidence.limits: Wind deflation removes upper salt-crust parapets in exposed desert playas.

evidence.title: Jiayuguan Fortress & Suspended Great Wall (Gansu): 1372 CE Ming Western Gate
evidence.dateBasis: Ming garrison bricks, loess ramparts & customs steles
evidence.summary: Sitting between the Qilian snow peaks and Black Mountain gorge, Jiayuguan anchored the Ming Empire's westernmost pass, regulating Central Asian horse-for-tea embassies.
evidence.limits: Outer rammed-earth apron walls required modern stabilization.

evidence.title: Yulin Zhenbeitai & Ming Yansui Great Wall (Shaanxi–Ordos Margin): Desert Garrison Frontier
evidence.dateBasis: Fort-network spatial modeling & Hongshan Horse Market
evidence.summary: Hundreds of walled beacon-forts along the Mu Us Desert rim regulated Ming–Mongol livestock fairs alongside military defense across shifting sand frontiers.
evidence.limits: Desertification buried intermediate curtain walls between watchtowers.

evidence.title: Badaling, Juyongguan & Cloud Terrace (Beijing): Imperial Capital Defense Gorge
evidence.dateBasis: Brick-and-granite masonry & Yuan hexa-script Cloud Terrace
evidence.summary: Guarding the rocky Guangou Gorge northwest of Beijing, Juyongguan's 1342 six-language Buddhist archway and Badaling's 16th-century double-walled ashlar parapets controlled steppe access to the imperial core.
evidence.limits: 1950s–1980s tourist restorations heavily rebuilt upper crenellations at Badaling.

evidence.title: Jinshanling, Mutianyu & Simatai Ridges (Hebei–Beijing): Qi Jiguang Hollow Watchtower System
evidence.dateBasis: Brick-kiln inscriptions & Ji-Town landscape archaeology
evidence.summary: General Qi Jiguang's 1568–1583 Ji-Town rebuild introduced two-story hollow brick watchtowers capable of quartering troops, crossfire artillery, and rapid optical signaling across steep Yanshan crests.
evidence.limits: Steep un-restored eastern ridges at Jinshanling preserve raw Ming brick fabric.

evidence.title: Shanhaiguan Pass & Laolongtou Sea Terminus (Bohai Coast, Hebei): First Pass Under Heaven
evidence.dateBasis: Granite sea-pier foundations & Ming–Qing transition records
evidence.summary: Anchoring the Ming Great Wall where Yanshan foothills plunge into the Bohai Sea—including the Old Dragon's Head granite jetty—Shanhaiguan controlled the Manchurian coastal corridor until 1644.
evidence.limits: Sea-pier timber piles suffered storm erosion prior to 20th-century reconstruction.

evidence.title: Huai'an Qingjiangpu Locks & Yangzhou Canal Docks (Jiangsu): Hydraulic Spine of China
evidence.dateBasis: Stone sluice gates, grain-barge registries & Yellow River levees
evidence.summary: Starting with King Fuchai's 486 BCE Han Conduit, pound locks at Huai'an solved the Yellow River–Huai watershed crossing, lifting millions of bushels of Yangtze rice and Huai salt north to Beijing.
evidence.limits: Repeated Yellow River avulsions repeatedly silted medieval channel alignments.

evidence.title: Kaifeng Northern Song Capital & Iron Pagoda (Henan): Million-Person Canal Metropolis
evidence.dateBasis: Stratified stacked cities beneath Yellow River silt; 1049 glaze pagoda
evidence.summary: Six superimposed urban strata buried under Yellow River flood silt preserve Kaifeng's Bian Canal bridges, coal-fired iron foundries, printed paper-money workshops, and the 1049 CE glazed Iron Pagoda.
evidence.limits: Deep water tables and historic flood deposits limit horizontal exposure of Song streets.

evidence.title: Nanjing 35-Kilometer Brick City Wall & Treasure Shipyard (Jiangsu): Early Ming Maritime Capital
evidence.dateBasis: Stamped brick maker inscriptions & dry-dock keel excavations
evidence.summary: Each kiln brick stamped with the responsible county official's name built Nanjing's 35 km perimeter alongside Longjiang dry-docks where Zheng He's treasure fleets were framed.
evidence.limits: Urban railway cuts opened breaches in eastern wall curtains in the 20th century.

evidence.title: Tang Luoyang Sui–Tang Grain Silos & Canal Quay (Henan): Subterranean Imperial Granaries
evidence.dateBasis: Hanjia Granary >250 circular storage pits & brick tally inscriptions
evidence.summary: Hanjia Granary's clay-lined underground silos held emergency grain delivered via the Sui Grand Canal from Jiangnan to provision eastern imperial courts.
evidence.limits: Urban expansion overlies southern outer wards of Sui–Tang Luoyang.

evidence.title: Tongguan Dragon Kilns (Changsha, Hunan): Mass Tang Painted Ceramic Exports
evidence.dateBasis: Kiln wasters matched to the 826 CE Belitung Indonesian shipwreck
evidence.summary: Over sixty hill-climbing dragon kilns along the Xiang River pioneered copper-red underglaze motifs, Arabic inscriptions, and Tang poetry on stoneware bowls exported to Basra and Java.
evidence.limits: Intensive medieval waster dumping mixed short-lived glaze batches.

evidence.title: Panlongcheng Shang River City & Hankou Tea Docks (Wuhan, Hubei): Middle Yangtze Hinge
evidence.dateBasis: Rammed-earth palace bronze hoards & 19th c. Russian brick-tea presses
evidence.summary: Panlongcheng controlled copper routes down the Han–Yangtze confluence during the Shang dynasty, while nearby Hankou later became China's interior steam-pressed brick-tea export hub to Siberia.
evidence.limits: Seasonal Yangtze floodplains require coring beneath modern levees.

evidence.title: Zigong Deep-Bore Salt Wells & Kangding Tea-Road Gateway (Sichuan): Percussion Drilling Heritage
evidence.dateBasis: Bamboo-cable percussion rigs & Shenhai 1,001-m borehole records
evidence.summary: Bamboo-and-iron percussion rigs drilled over 1,000 meters for natural brine and methane fuel in Zigong, financing guilds linked uphill via Ya'an and Kangding into Tibetan Tea Horse caravans.
evidence.limits: Modern saltworks replaced wooden derricks after 1900 except preserved Shenhai.

evidence.title: Jingmai Ancient Tea Forests, Pu'er & Lijiang Dayan (Yunnan): Origin Hub of the Tea Horse Road
evidence.dateBasis: Palaung–Dai forest agroecology & flagstone mule tracks
evidence.summary: Understory tea groves tended by Blang and Dai communities in Jingmai and Pu'er supplied compressed tea cakes hauled north by Naxi and Tibetan muleteers through Lijiang and Shangri-La.
evidence.limits: Subtropical forest soils obscure pre-Ming mule stations outside paved towns.

evidence.title: Dukezong (Shangri-La) & Deqin Pass (NW Yunnan–Kham): Steep Gorge Corridor to Lhasa
evidence.dateBasis: Bridge abutments, caravan inns & Yunnan–Tibet customs records
evidence.summary: Caravans climbed from 1,800-meter Jinsha River gorges across 4,300-meter snow passes through Dukezong to exchange compressed Yunnan tea for Tibetan horses, wool, salt, and medicinal herbs.
evidence.limits: Landslides along the Jinsha and Lancang canyons frequently cut medieval trailbeds.

evidence.title: Pingyao Banking Walled City & Qixian Yards (Shanxi): Draft-Bank Finance Along the Tea Road
evidence.dateBasis: Rishengchang ledger archives & Ming courtyard walls
evidence.summary: Shanxi *piaohao* draft banks headquartered inside Pingyao's Ming ramparts issued silver remittances spanning Canton, Hankou, and Kiakhta, underwriting Eurasian tea and fur finance.
evidence.limits: Early 17th-century ledger archives before Rishengchang (1823) are fragmentary.

evidence.title: Hami Oasis & Turpan Karez Qanat Shafts (Xinjiang): Subterranean Desert Hydraulics
evidence.dateBasis: OSL quartz dates & snowmelt tunnel geometry
evidence.summary: Over 1,100 underground *karez* gravity tunnels tapped Flaming Mountain snowmelt beneath evaporation zones to sustain oasis cotton, grapes, and Silk Road caravan stables.
evidence.limits: Active maintenance by oasis farmers continually recuts vertical access shafts.

evidence.title: Guihua (Hohhot) & Fengzhou Tumet Courtyard City (Inner Mongolia): Steppe–Ming Market Peace
evidence.dateBasis: Altan Khan monastic brickwork & horse-fair treaties
evidence.summary: Founded by Altan Khan beside the Daqing Mountains after the 1571 Longqing Accord, Guihua transformed armed Great Wall tension into regulated horse, silk, and iron markets.
evidence.limits: Urban growth in modern Hohhot overlays peripheral 16th-century yurts and market stalls.

evidence.title: Yuegang (Moon Harbor, Zhangzhou, Fujian): Late Ming Silver–Silk Galleon Hub
evidence.dateBasis: Zhangzhou kiln blue-and-white sherds & Manila customs logs
evidence.summary: Legalized for private overseas junk voyages in 1567, Moon Harbor dispatched silk, tea, and Kraak porcelain directly to Manila and Nagasaki in exchange for New World and Japanese silver.
evidence.limits: Estuarine siltation shifted international ocean shipping to Xiamen after the 1680s.

evidence.title: Nanhai Shenmiao Port Temple & Huaisheng Minaret (Guangzhou): Tang–Song Monsoon Harbor
evidence.dateBasis: Coastal stele inscriptions, ship-tax annals & mosque tower
evidence.summary: Centuries before Canton's Thirteen Factories, Maritime Customs Offices and foreign merchant quarters around Guangzhou's Huaisheng Mosque anchored China's western Indian Ocean gateway.
evidence.limits: Silted Pearl River distributaries place Tang quays far inland from modern docks.

evidence.title: Longxingsi Hoard & Maritime Penglai Fortress (Shandong): North China Sea–Korea Hinge
evidence.dateBasis: Polychrome limestone Buddha cache & Penglai Water City warships
evidence.summary: Qingzhou's painted Northern Wei–Northern Qi sculptures and Penglai's walled Ming naval harbor link inland Central Plain workshops with Yellow Sea naval and commercial routes to Korea and Japan.
evidence.limits: 12th-century iconoclastic burial mixed dates across statues inside the cache pit.

evidence.title: Quanzhou Kaiyuan Temple & Luoyang Tidal Oyster Bridge (Fujian): 1059 CE Engineering
evidence.dateBasis: Biochemical oyster-cemented granite piers & bilingual tombstones
evidence.summary: Builder Cai Xiang cultivated reef oysters to cement the 831-meter Luoyang tidal stone bridge north of Quanzhou, linking Song Fujian's kiln hinterland to Arabic, Tamil, and Persian merchant docks.
evidence.limits: Repairs to upper deck slabs overlaid Song piers with Yuan–Ming stonework.

evidence.title: Shaxi Sideng Market & Bai Caravan Courtyard (Jianchuan, Yunnan): Intact Tea-Horse Hub
evidence.dateBasis: Shibaoshan Grottoes & cobbled Bai bazaar architecture
evidence.summary: Protected inside a high mountain basin, Shaxi preserves an intact Nanzhao–Ming–Qing caravan theater square and mud-brick inns along the western branch of the Yunnan–Tibet Tea Horse Road.
evidence.limits: Modern flood controls altered original wooden footbridge approaches prior to restoration.

evidence.title: Ninguta (Ning'an) & Mudan River Frontier Stockade (Heilongjiang): Qing Amur Staging Base
evidence.dateBasis: Willow Palisade maps & Qing river-fleet logbooks
evidence.summary: Guarding the Jurchen homeland behind the Willow Palisade, Ninguta supplied grain, river boats, and Solon–Manchu bannermen for the Amur frontier campaigns culminating at Albazin.
evidence.limits: Timber stockade foundations lie beneath modern Ning'an streets.

evidence.title: Ding Kilns (Quyang, Hebei) & Handan Cizhou Ware: Northern White Porcelain Industry
evidence.dateBasis: Coal-fired horse-shoe kilns & impressed floral whiteware
evidence.summary: Pioneering coal-fired high-temperature stoneware and delicate ivory-white porcelain, Ding Kilns supplied Liao steppe courts, Song elites, and Silk Road exports prior to Jingdezhen's hegemony.
evidence.limits: Kiln mounds suffered agricultural cutting before heritage protection.

evidence.title: Hailongtun Mountain Tusi Citadel (Zunyi, Guizhou): SW Frontier Autonomy (1257–1600 CE)
evidence.dateBasis: 36-step limestone cliff gates & 1600 Ming siege ruins
evidence.summary: Perched atop razorback karst ridges in Guizhou, the Yang hereditary *tusi* chiefdom defended autonomous Miao–Gelao mountain corridors linking Sichuan to Lingnan until crushed in 1600.
evidence.limits: Humid subtropical vegetation obscures outer wooden palisade postholes.

evidence.title: Kashgar Ancient Bazaar & Apak Khoja Enclosure (Western Tarim, Xinjiang): Pamir Gateway
evidence.dateBasis: Ramming-loess old city mounds & multilingual manuscript fragments
evidence.summary: Positioned at the junction of the Northern and Southern Silk Roads beneath the Pamir passes, Kashgar linked Sogdian, Karakhanid, Uyghur, and Qing caravan trails toward Samarkand and Leh.
evidence.limits: 20th-century mudbrick renewals replaced earlier medieval facade strata.

evidence.title: West Lake Dikes & Fenghuangshan Imperial Precinct (Hangzhou): Southern Song Seat (1138–1276)
evidence.dateBasis: Excavated imperial avenues, Shuidao culverts & Marco Polo descriptions
evidence.summary: Rebuilt as the Southern Song capital after the loss of Kaifeng, Hangzhou paired Grand Canal terminal wharves, paper-money printing, and Guan Imperial celadon kilns for maritime trade.
evidence.limits: Excavations remain localized beneath dense historic downtown Hangzhou.

evidence.title: Baxiandong (Changbin Caves, Taitung): ~30–15 ka Uplifted Sea-Cave Foragers
evidence.dateBasis: AMS charcoal dates inside raised wave-cut basalt caves
evidence.summary: Unifacial pebble choppers and quartz flakes on eastern Taiwan's uplifted marine terraces confirm Late Pleistocene coastal foragers crossing from mainland shelves at glacial low sea stands.
evidence.limits: Acidic cave drip-water dissolved human and faunal skeletal remains.

evidence.title: Eluanbi / O-luan-pi Southern Cape Dunes (Pingtung, Taiwan): 5,000 BP Maritime Bridge
evidence.dateBasis: Calcareous sand stratigraphy, shell adzes & slate-cist burials
evidence.summary: Facing the Bashi Channel toward Batanes and Luzon, Eluanbi's red-corded pottery and Tridacna shell-tool workshops chart early Austronesian voyaging adaptations south of Taiwan.
evidence.limits: Coastal typhoons rework dune strata near coral benches.

evidence.title: Shihsanhang Iron-Smelting Coastal Town (Bali District, New Taipei): 1,800–500 BP Trade
evidence.dateBasis: Slag bloomery furnaces, Indo-Pacific beads & Tang bronze coins
evidence.summary: Excavated iron-smelting furnaces, Song–Tang Chinese coins, and agate beads along the Tamsui Estuary document indigenous Ketagalan participation in South and East China Sea maritime exchange.
evidence.limits: Urban sewage-plant grading rescued only the preserved core sector.

evidence.title: Anping (Fort Zeelandia) & Provintia Harbour (Tainan, Taiwan): 17th c. Sugar–Deer–Porcelain Pivot
evidence.dateBasis: Dutch/Ming–Qing brick foundations & VOC shipping ledgers
evidence.summary: Built on the Tayouan sandbar across from Fujian, Anping bridged Hakka–Hoklo settlers, Siraya deer hunters, Zheng Chenggong's maritime realm, and Dutch–Japanese silver–silk shipping.
evidence.limits: Tainan coastal progradation has placed the historic sandbar port several kilometers inland.

evidence.title: Lukang Harbor Streets & Longshan Timber Halls (Changhua, Taiwan): Qing Cross-Strait Guilds
evidence.dateBasis: Quanzhou-guild stone inscriptions & Fujian timber framing
evidence.summary: Opposite Quanzhou across the Taiwan Strait, Lukang's *jiao* merchant guilds exported deerskins, camphor, sugar, and rice while importing Fujian stone ballast, ceramic tiles, and guild temples.
evidence.limits: River mouth silting ended ocean-going junk anchorage in the 1840s.

evidence.title: Tolbor-4 & Tolbor-21 River Terraces (Selenge Basin, N. Mongolia): 45–25 ka IUP Blades
evidence.dateBasis: OSL loess dates & ostrich-eggshell bead radiocarbon
evidence.summary: Long stratified sequences along the Tolbor Valley track Initial Upper Paleolithic laminar blades, ostrich-eggshell ornaments, and modern human dispersal corridors linking Altai, Mongolia, and Baikal.
evidence.limits: Loess cryoturbation subtly shifts micro-lenses at terrace margins.

evidence.title: Tsatsyn Ereg & Khoid Tamir Khirigsuur–Deer Stone Sanctuary (Arkhangai): Horse Rituals
evidence.dateBasis: Equine sacrifice satellite-mound C14 & laser scans
evidence.summary: Over a hundred satellite stone mounds containing east-facing horse skulls surround monumental khirigsuur cairns and flying-stag steles, revealing communal Bronze Age pastoralist feasting and riding.
evidence.limits: Surface exposure of basalt slabs accelerates lichen weathering on stag reliefs.

evidence.title: Khöshöö Tsaidam (Kül Tigin & Bilge Khagan Steles, Orkhon Valley): 732–735 CE Runic Texts
evidence.dateBasis: Bilingual Old Turkic Runic–Tang Chinese steles & marble turtles
evidence.summary: Bilingual royal inscriptions of the Second Turkic Khaganate in the Orkhon meadow commemorate steppe campaigns, political philosophy, and the earliest deciphered indigenous Turkic alphabet.
evidence.limits: Burial vaults behind the sacrificial shrines remain subject to preservation rules.

evidence.title: Tamiryn Ulaan Khoshuu & Slab Grave Horizon (Central Mongolia): Xiongnu Ancestor Turnover
evidence.dateBasis: Ancient DNA trajectories & bronze-iron metallurgy
evidence.summary: Rectangular slab-lined graves and multi-ethnic Xiongnu cemeteries trace a major genetic and political unification uniting Eastern Steppe Slab Grave herders with Western Altai Scythian-Sarmatian groups.
evidence.limits: High-visibility stone slabs invited post-Bronze Age reuse in satellite burials.

evidence.title: Khar Bukh Balgas Khitan Frontier Fortress (Bulgan): 10th–11th c. Steppe Brick City
evidence.dateBasis: Liao–Khitan ramparts & birch-bark Legal Code hoard
evidence.summary: Garrisoned by the Liao Khitan dynasty across central Mongolia and reoccupied by 17th-century Khalkha monks whose stupa concealed Mongol-Oirat birch-bark law manuscripts.
evidence.limits: Arid wind erosion affects unbaked mudbrick cores outside stone temple foundations.

evidence.title: Khar Khul Khaany Balgas (Khanui Valley, Arkhangai): 13th–14th c. Mongol Urban Node
evidence.dateBasis: Geophysical magnetometry, Yuan roof tiles & kiln trenches
evidence.summary: Unchronicled in European travelogues, this fortified valley city in north-central Mongolia hosted elite Mongol courtyard halls, craft kilns, and seasonal imperial logistics outside Karakorum.
evidence.limits: Only selective test trenches have sampled its gridded compounds.

evidence.title: Amarbayasgalant Monastery (Iven River Valley, Selenge): 1727–1736 Zanabazar Sanctuary
evidence.dateBasis: Manchu–Tibetan–Mongol courtyard timber architecture
evidence.summary: Constructed in the Selenge foothills as a memorial sanctuary for sculptor-patriarch Zanabazar, its symmetrical brick and timber halls housed thousands of monks and woodblock printing presses.
evidence.limits: 1930s purges destroyed outlying ger-monastic quarters before core restoration.

evidence.title: Ikh Khüree / Urga (Tuul Valley, Ulaanbaatar): 1639–1900 Mobile Monastic to Fixed Capital
evidence.dateBasis: 28 nomadic relocations log & Gandantegchinlen–Maimaicheng quarters
evidence.summary: After relocating 28 times across steppe pastures between 1639 and 1778, the Bogd Gegen's monastic camp settled beside the Tuul River as Mongolia's diplomatic, tea-road, and religious capital.
evidence.limits: Seasonal felt-ger encampments left light subsurface footprints prior to 19th-century brick districts.

evidence.title: Tsagaan Salaa–Baga Oigor Rock Art (Bayan-Ölgii, Mongolian Altai): 10,000+ High-Valley Carvings
evidence.dateBasis: Glacial bedrock polish & Chariot/Turkic stylistic seriation
evidence.summary: More than ten thousand glacial-boulder engravings near Tavan Bogd document snow-leopard hunters, Bronze Age chariots, deer stones, and Turkic riders along Altai mountain passes.
evidence.limits: Direct chronological dating of surface varnish remains stylistic rather than AMS.

evidence.title: Khovd Sangiiin Kherem & Uliastai Garrisons (Western Mongolia): Zunghar–Qing Steppe Hub
evidence.dateBasis: Rammed-earth garrison walls & Irkutsk–Altai trade ledgers
evidence.summary: Guarding the Altai corridors connecting Xinjiang oases to southern Siberia, Khovd and Uliastai channeled Kazakh, Oirat, Russian, and Chinese brick-tea caravans across western Mongolia.
evidence.limits: Rammed-earth Sangiiin Kherem perimeter walls eroded heavily after 1911.

evidence.title: Zuunkhangai & Khuvsgul Deer-Stone Basins (NW Mongolia): Basalt Quarry & Steppe Sanctuaries
evidence.dateBasis: Petrographic XRF sourcing & 3D photogrammetry
evidence.summary: Petrographic sourcing of sculpted deer stones in Uvs and Khuvsgul shows pastoral kin groups quarried and hauled two-ton granite steles across river valleys to anchor seasonal clan territories.
evidence.limits: Deep burial of lower carved bands leaves some weapon belts underground.

evidence.title: Chinggis Khan's Northern Arc Wall (Dornod–Khentii): 11th–12th c. Jin/Khitan Border Trench
evidence.dateBasis: Satellite trench mapping, Liao–Jin sherds & soil micromorphology
evidence.summary: Stretching hundreds of kilometers across northeastern Mongolia's open forest-steppe, an earthen dyke and regularly spaced garrison enclosures controlled seasonal pastoral migrations rather than siege armies.
evidence.limits: Low earthen embankments appear clearly in drone/satellite imagery rather than vertical ruins.

evidence.title: Iwajuku Loam Quarry (Midori, Gunma): 1949 Discovery of Japan's 35 ka Paleolithic
evidence.dateBasis: Kanto volcanic tephra & obsidian hydration
evidence.summary: Aizawa Tadahiro's 1949 find of edge-ground stone axes and obsidian backed blades inside Kanto volcanic loam overturned the orthodoxy of no pre-Jōmon Ice Age settlement in Japan.
evidence.limits: Acidic volcanic loam dissolves non-siliceous organic artifacts.

evidence.title: Torihama Shell Midden (Wakasa, Fukui): Early Jōmon Lacquerware, Comb & Dugout Canoes
evidence.dateBasis: AMS seed/lacquer dates in anaerobic lake peat
evidence.summary: Waterlogged Lake Mikata peat preserves bright cinnabar-red *urushi* lacquer combs, cedar-log canoes, domesticated bottle gourds, and woven cordage 6,000 years before rice agriculture.
evidence.limits: Only low-lying lakeside trenches retain delicate botanical fibers.

evidence.title: Makimuku & Hashihaka Tomb (Sakurai, Nara): 3rd c. CE Proto-Urban Yamato Hub
evidence.dateBasis: Calibrated dendro/AMS pottery & non-local ceramic counts
evidence.summary: Excavations across Makimuku revealed monumental wooden halls, peach pits from ritual feasts, and 280-meter keyhole Hashihaka tumulus containing pottery from every region from Kyushu to Kanto.
evidence.limits: Imperial Household Agency restrictions bar internal excavation of Hashihaka's burial chamber.

evidence.title: Dazaifu Government Precinct & 664 CE Mizuki Water Rampart (Fukuoka): Western Gate
evidence.dateBasis: 1.2-km timber-cored earthen dam & Korokan envoy guesthouse
evidence.summary: After the 663 CE Baekgang battle, the Yamato court erected Dazaifu's kilometer-long moated Mizuki dam and the Hakata Korokan hostel to guard Kyushu and manage Tang–Silla–Goryeo trade missions.
evidence.limits: Suburban growth overlaid outer residential grids outside the preserved government hall.

evidence.title: Heian-kyō Palace Precincts & Uji Byōdō-in (Kyoto, 794–1185 CE): Aristocratic Court Culture
evidence.dateBasis: 1053 CE Phoenix Hall timber & Heian aristocratic manor trenches
evidence.summary: Gridded on Chang'an geometry, Heian-kyō cultivated *kana* literature, woodblock temple arts, and Fujiwara court estates while provincial *bushi* warrior bands rose across eastern Honshu.
evidence.limits: Dense modern Kyoto restricts exposure of the inner Daidairi palace blocks.

evidence.title: Kamakura Shogunate Precinct & Wakaejima Stone Jetty (Kanagawa, 1185–1333 CE): First Bakufu
evidence.dateBasis: Excavated Yuigahama samurai compounds, imported Song celadon & harbor breakwater
evidence.summary: Minamoto no Yoritomo established Japan's first military shogunate (*bakufu*) inside Kamakura's mountain-enclosed basin, codifying samurai land law (*Goseibai Shikimoku*) while trading Song copper coins.
evidence.limits: Tsunamis and 14th-century sieges scarred coastal timber wards.

evidence.title: Hakata Bay Genkō Bōrui Stone Seawall (Fukuoka): 1276–1281 Anti-Mongol Coastal Rampart
evidence.dateBasis: 20-km quarried granite seawall & Yuan shipwreck munitions
evidence.summary: Mobilized by the Kamakura shogunate between the 1274 and 1281 Mongol invasions, provincial samurai vassals built a 20-kilometer stone coastal curtain across Hakata Bay that denied Yuan cavalry landing beaches.
evidence.limits: Coastal reclamation buried most sectors beneath modern Fukuoka seawalls.

evidence.title: Muromachi Kyoto (Hana-no-Gosho, Kinkaku-ji & Ginkaku-ji, 1336–1573 CE): Ashikaga Shogunate
evidence.dateBasis: Ashikaga palace excavations, Ming tally-trade records & Zen gardens
evidence.summary: Ruling from Kyoto's Muromachi district, Ashikaga shoguns patronized Zen aesthetics, Noh theater, tea ceremony, and Ming tally-ships (*kangōsen*), before the 1467–1477 Ōnin War fractured provinces into Warring States.
evidence.limits: Ōnin street fighting burned the original Hana-no-Gosho palace structures.

evidence.title: Azuchi Castle Stone Ramparts & Honmaru Plan (Ōmihachiman, Shiga, 1576): Tenshu Prototype
evidence.dateBasis: Gold-leafed roof tiles, *ishigaki* masonry & archival floor plans
evidence.summary: Built by Oda Nobunaga overlooking Lake Biwa's main Kyoto approach, Azuchi pioneered towering dressed-stone *ishigaki* ramparts, a multistory *tenshu* donjon, and an open-market merchant town (*rakuichi-rakuza*).
evidence.limits: Destroyed by fire in 1582 immediately after the Honnō-ji Incident.

evidence.title: Osaka Castle (Ōsaka-jō) Megalithic Bastions & 1614–1615 Siege Ruins (Osaka): Unification Crucible
evidence.dateBasis: Buried Toyotomi gold-leaf stonework beneath Tokugawa granite walls
evidence.summary: Toyotomi Hideyoshi's golden fortress and the massive 1615 siege ditches uncovered beneath Tokugawa Ieyasu's towering granite ramparts chronicle the decisive transition from civil war to Edo hegemony.
evidence.limits: 1931 concrete donjon covers the reconstructed inner keep summit.

evidence.title: Sekigahara Pass Battlefield & Nakasendō Chokepoint (Gifu, 1600 CE): Dawn of Edo Rule
evidence.dateBasis: Matchlock earthworks, heraldic banners & Tokugawa battle maps
evidence.summary: Between Mount Ibuki and the Nakasendō pass, Tokugawa Ieyasu's Eastern coalition defeated Ishida Mitsunari's Western army in 1600, enabling the 1603 founding of the 265-year Tokugawa Shogunate.
evidence.limits: Fog and shifting battle lines leave earthwork traces mainly on flank hilltops.

evidence.title: Edo Castle Inner Moats & Daimyō Yashiki Quarters (Tokyo, 1603–1868 CE): Bakufu Metropolis
evidence.dateBasis: Izu-quarried ashlar stone walls, waterworks & Marunouchi yashiki excavations
evidence.summary: Expanding into a million-resident capital through spiral moats and mandatory *sankin-kōtai* daimyō domain compounds, Edo Castle served as the bureaucratic nerve center of Tokugawa peace and early modern urbanization.
evidence.limits: 1657 Meireki Fire burned Edo's five-tier main *tenshu*, never rebuilt.

evidence.title: Nijō Castle (Ninomaru Palace & Nightingale Floors, Kyoto, 1603–1867 CE): Shogunal Residence
evidence.dateBasis: Kanō school sliding screen art, moats & 1867 *Taisei Hōkan* proclamation
evidence.summary: Constructed beside Kyoto's Imperial Palace by Tokugawa Ieyasu as his western residence, Nijō's gilded Ninomaru chambers witnessed both 17th-century shogunal grandeur and the 1867 return of sovereignty to the Emperor.
evidence.limits: Original 1626 *tenshu* keep struck by lightning in 1750.

evidence.title: Matsumoto Castle (Karasu-jō, Nagano, 1593–1594 CE): Oldest Five-Tiered Timber Keep
evidence.dateBasis: Dendrochronology of original six-story interior cypress framework
evidence.summary: Rising above flat-plain water moats in the Japanese Alps, Matsumoto's black-clapboard *tenshu* pairs gunports and stone-drop chutes with later moon-viewing verandas reflecting peaceful Edo rule.
evidence.limits: Foundation subsidence beneath moat piles required full timber dismantling and restoration in 1903–1913.

evidence.title: Inuyama-jō (1537/1601) & Hikone-jō (1622) Original Timber Tenshu (Aichi–Shiga)
evidence.dateBasis: Original Edo carpentry joinery & Lake Biwa/Kiso River granite bastions
evidence.summary: Guarding the Kiso River cliffs and Lake Biwa's eastern Nakasendō road respectively, Inuyama and Hikone preserve intact pre-1868 wooden keeps and bell-tower garrisons overlooking strategic highways.
evidence.limits: Outer residential rings were cleared during Meiji demilitarization.

evidence.title: Kumamoto Castle Curved Musha-gaeshi Ramparts & Matsue-jō Keep (Kyushu–Shimane, 1607–1611)
evidence.dateBasis: Katō Kiyomasa parabolic stone walls & 1877 Satsuma siege scars
evidence.summary: Kumamoto's steeply curving basalt walls withstood the 1877 Satsuma Rebellion for fifty days, while Matsue's dark-boarded San'in keep survives as one of Japan's twelve original pre-1868 castle towers.
evidence.limits: 2016 earthquake damaged portions of Kumamoto's historic masonry.

evidence.title: Bitchū Matsuyama, Marugame & Uwajima Mountain Keeps (Seto Inland Sea): Original Tenshu
evidence.dateBasis: Highest surviving *yamajiro* keep (430 m) & Inland Sea port citadels
evidence.summary: Along the Seto Inland Sea salt-and-maritime lanes, surviving original Edo keeps at Bitchū Matsuyama (highest surviving mountain castle) and Marugame illustrate transition from hilltop bastions to maritime ports.
evidence.limits: Several lower baileys were turned into public parks after the 1873 Castle Abolition Edict.

evidence.title: Nakijin, Zakimi & Katsuren Ryukyuan Gusuku Castles (Okinawa): 14th–15th c. Limestone Forts
evidence.dateBasis: Sinuous Ryukyuan limestone masonry, Longquan celadon & SE Asian sherds
evidence.summary: Before Chūzan unification, regional Okinawan *aji* lords raised curving coral-limestone *gusuku* hillforts stocked with Yuan–Ming celadon, Vietnamese ceramics, and Southeast Asian spices.
evidence.limits: Upper wooden halls vanished leaving curved masonry walls and sacred *utaki* groves.

evidence.title: Tōkaidō Hakone Barrier & Nakasendō Kiso Post-Towns (Kanagawa–Nagano): Shogunal Highways
evidence.dateBasis: Cedar-lined stone *ishidatami* paving & *sekisho* passport registries
evidence.summary: Five regulated *Gokaidō* highways funnelled massive *sankin-kōtai* daimyō processions, pilgrims, courier dispatches, and woodblock-print commerce between Edo, Kyoto, and Nagasaki.
evidence.limits: Meiji railways and motor roads bypassed most intact post-town timber streets.

evidence.title: Iwami Ginzan Silver Mines (Shimane) & Sado Gold Complex (Niigata): 16th–19th c. Bullion
evidence.dateBasis: Cupellation ash-smelting slag, hand-chiseled adits & Edo mint ledgers
evidence.summary: Iwami Ginzan and Sado supplied roughly one-third of world silver output around 1600, underwriting Ming porcelain purchases, *shuinsen* Southeast Asian trade, and Tokugawa state coinage.
evidence.limits: Deep subterranean levels flooded when pre-modern bamboo pumps ceased.

evidence.title: Sakata Honma Docks & Kanazawa Castle-Town (Sea of Japan): Kitamaebune Coastal Shipping
evidence.dateBasis: Sankyo rice granaries, timber *bezaisen* records & lacquerware
evidence.summary: Flat-bottomed coastal *kitamaebune* cargo ships rounded western Honshu linking Osaka wholesalers with Hokuriku, Dewa rice barns in Sakata, and Hokkaido herring fisheries.
evidence.limits: Modern steel harbors replaced wooden coastal river wharves.

evidence.title: Matsumae Castle (Oshima) & Nibutani Saru River (Hokkaido): Ainu–Shogunate Frontier Trade
evidence.dateBasis: Matsumae trade-post logs & *chashi* earthen ridge forts
evidence.summary: As Japan's northernmost Edo castle-domain, Matsumae brokered salmon, kelp, hawk feathers, and Amur silk goods between Ainu *kotan* communities and Honshu rice merchants.
evidence.limits: Meiji colonization after 1869 heavily disrupted traditional Ainu riverine autonomy.

evidence.title: Yokohama Treaty Port & Tomioka Silk Reeling Mill (Kanagawa–Gunma): 1859–1900 Industrial Shift
evidence.dateBasis: Timber-brick steam reeling bays & Silk Road maritime customs ledgers
evidence.summary: Opening immediately after the dismantling of Tokugawa maritime restrictions, Tomioka's French-equipped steam reeling sheds and Yokohama's docks vaulted Japan into global industrial textiles.
evidence.limits: 1923 Great Kantō Earthquake destroyed many 1860s Yokohama masonry warehouses.

evidence.title: Seokjang-ni Geum River Terraces (Gongju, South Chungcheong): Stratified Paleolithic Sequence
evidence.dateBasis: Alluvial terrace stratigraphy & tanged-point blade horizons
evidence.summary: Twelve Pleistocene occupation levels spanning pebble choppers, handaxes, and Late Paleolithic blade hearths make Seokjang-ni the founding chronological benchmark of Korean Peninsula archaeology.
evidence.limits: Acidic riverine soils leave little unburned Pleistocene faunal bone.

evidence.title: Bibong-ri Wetland Shell Midden (Changnyeong, South Gyeongsang): 8,000-Year Pine Canoe
evidence.dateBasis: AMS wood dating on charred-dugout pine & woven basketry
evidence.summary: Tidal-mud preservation at Bibong-ri yielded the Korean Peninsula's oldest dugout watercraft (~8,000 cal BP) alongside acorn storage pits, woven nets, and wild boar bones.
evidence.limits: Ancient estuarine bay silted inland away from the modern Nakdong shore.

evidence.title: Bangudae River Cliff Petroglyphs (Ulsan): Neolithic–Bronze Age Whale Hunting Panels
evidence.dateBasis: Sub-style superposition of harpooned whales & netted boats
evidence.summary: Carved onto vertical shale above the Daegokcheon bend, over 300 motifs depict North Pacific right whales, gray whales, boats with crews, and wild deer—documenting early coastal whaling.
evidence.limits: Seasonal fluctuations of the downstream Sayeon Dam reservoir submerge lower registers.

evidence.title: Anhak Palace & Taesong Mountain Fortress (Pyongyang): Goguryeo Southern Capital (427–668 CE)
evidence.dateBasis: Kilometer-wide mountain stone curtain, tile seals & painted chamber tombs
evidence.summary: Goguryeo shifted its capital from the Yalu gorges south to Anhak and Taesong Fortress above the Taedong River, pairing defensive mountain citadels with astronomical tomb murals.
evidence.limits: Upper wooden palatial halls vanished beneath post-668 agricultural terraces.

evidence.title: Gongsanseong Fortress & Iksan Mireuksa Granite Pagoda (Gongju–Iksan): Baekje Capitals
evidence.dateBasis: Royal Tomb of King Muryeong (525 CE) & Baekje granite ashlar masonry
evidence.summary: After moving down the Geum River to Gongju and Iksan, Baekje kings built mountain river fortresses, China–Japan Buddhist diplomatic missions, and Korea's oldest surviving monumental granite pagoda.
evidence.limits: Repeated siege repairs blended Baekje, Silla, and Joseon masonry courses.

evidence.title: Bulguksa Stone Terraces & Seokguram Granite Grotto (Gyeongju): 751 CE Unified Silla
evidence.dateBasis: Corbelled granite dome geometry & Silla royal tomb genomics
evidence.summary: Dry-fitted interlocking stone terraces at Bulguksa and Seokguram's domed Mount Toham granite shrine synthesized Silk Road Gandharan–Tang sculpture with Silla precision geometry.
evidence.limits: Wooden pavilion halls at Bulguksa were rebuilt after 1592 wartime burning atop original 8th-century stone plinths.

evidence.title: Heungdeoksa Temple Foundry (Cheongju): 1377 CE Jikji Earliest Surviving Metal-Type Book
evidence.dateBasis: Excavated monastic bronze bell, drum & colophon of *Jikji* (1377)
evidence.summary: Casting bronze-alloy movable type seventy-eight years before Gutenberg's press, monks at Heungdeoksa printed *Jikji*, extending Goryeo movable metal-type printing documented as early as 1234.
evidence.limits: Original type matrices dispersed; surviving Volume II is preserved in Paris.

evidence.title: Hansando & Myeongnyang Strait (Tongyeong–Jindo): 1592–1597 Imjin Naval Chokepoints
evidence.dateBasis: Tidal-current bathymetry, *panokseon* cannon ordnance & Admiral Yi war diaries
evidence.summary: Using armored *panokseon* and turtle-ship (*geobukseon*) broadsides against fierce tidal narrows, Joseon Admiral Yi Sun-sin severed Toyotomi Hideyoshi's sea supply lines across southern Korea.
evidence.limits: 16th-century wooden wrecks lie dispersed beneath swift southern straits.

evidence.title: Namhansanseong Mountain Fortress (Gwangju, Gyeonggi): 1624–1637 Emergency Capital Citadel
evidence.dateBasis: 12-km granite ridge wall, monk-soldier barracks & Manchu siege records
evidence.summary: Incorporating earlier Silla masonry into a 12-kilometer walled mountain basin manned by Buddhist monk militias, Namhansanseong shielded the Joseon court during the 1636–1637 Qing winter siege.
evidence.limits: Upper rampart crenellations underwent restoration following colonial-era neglect.

evidence.title: Andong Hahoe Confucian Village & Jeju Haenyeo Commons: Joseon Clan & Maritime Society
evidence.dateBasis: Nakdong River clan lineage houses, Seowon academies & Jeju dive-harvest logs
evidence.summary: River-encircled Hahoe scholar-gentry compounds preserve Joseon Confucian clan printing and mask drama, complementing Jeju's female *haenyeo* breath-hold kelp and abalone guilds.
evidence.limits: Thatch and timber courtyard structures require regular cyclical renewal.

evidence.title: Saraishyk / Saray-Jük (Lower Ural River, Atyrau, Kazakhstan): Golden Horde Silk City
evidence.dateBasis: Ceramic water-pipes, khans' mausolea & Coin mints
evidence.summary: Bridging the Ural crossing between Sarai on the Volga and Khwarazmian Urgench, Saraishyk operated ceramic aqueducts, caravan baths, and early Kazakh Khanate royal tombs.
evidence.limits: Ural River meanders are actively eroding the southeastern quarter of the tell.

evidence.title: Shilikty & Eleke Sazy Royal Kurgans (East Kazakhstan–Tarbagatai): 8th–7th c. BCE Saka Gold
evidence.dateBasis: Radiocarbon wood & Scythian–Saka animal-style gold plaques
evidence.summary: Over 4,000 cast and foil snow-leopard, argali, and deer gold emblems from Shilikty Kurgan 5 rank among the oldest monumental Early Saka royal burials across the Tarbagatai Steppe.
evidence.limits: Stone robber shafts penetrated several central burial chambers in antiquity.

evidence.title: Akyrtas Red-Sandstone Palace Foundation (Zhambyl, Southern Kazakhstan): Karluk Mega-Block Citadel
evidence.dateBasis: 1.5-ton cut sandstone blocks, clay aqueducts & Karluk stratigraphy
evidence.summary: Massive unfinished red-sandstone ashlar foundations covering 3.5 hectares along the northern Tien Shan foothills mark an ambitious 8th–9th century Karluk palace and caravan hub near Taraz.
evidence.limits: Construction halted before upper vaulted ceilings were completed.

evidence.title: Talgar Walled Oasis Town (Almaty Piedmont, Kazakhstan): Steel-Forging Tian Shan Gateway
evidence.dateBasis: Crucible steel ingots, cobble streets & irrigation canals
evidence.summary: Commanding snowmelt alluvial fans above the Ili Steppe, Talgar workshops smelted crucible Damascus-style steel and traded apples, grain, and textiles with pastoralists and Chinese merchants.
evidence.limits: Alluvial fans and modern town edges overlap outer suburban kiln fields.

evidence.title: Merke Alpine Balbal Sanctuaries & Karatau Arpauzen Petroglyphs (Southern Kazakhstan)
evidence.dateBasis: High-pasture Turkic granite steles & Bronze-Age chariot panels
evidence.summary: At 3,000 meters above sea level in the Kyrgyz Alatau meadows, carved Turkic stone *balbal* steles and Karatau chariot engravings preserve sacred summer-pasture assemblies spanning 2,500 years.
evidence.limits: High-mountain lichen and seasonal snow-creep limit subsurface organics.

evidence.title: Zarautsoy Grottoes (Kugitangtau Gorge, Surkhandarya, Uzbekistan): Mesolithic Ibex Hunts
evidence.dateBasis: Stylistic red-ochre superpositions & microlithic floor levels
evidence.summary: More than two hundred red-ochre paintings in limestone gorges depict cloaked hunters with dogs stalking wild ibex, aurochs, and gazelles overlooking the Amu Darya piedmont.
evidence.limits: Ochre mineral binders lack direct radiocarbon collagen for pinpoint C14 assays.

evidence.title: Djarkutan (Jarkutan, Surkhandarya, Uzbekistan): 2000 BCE Oxus Citadel & Fire Temple
evidence.dateBasis: BMAC mudbrick palace, kiln quarters & AMS wheat/barley dates
evidence.summary: Covering over 100 hectares on the Sherabad alluvial plain, Djarkutan anchors the northern Bactria–Margiana Archaeological Complex with a monumental fire temple, bronze seals, and Early Iron shifts.
evidence.limits: Irrigated modern cotton fields trimmed eastern craft quarters.

evidence.title: Toprak-Kala & Ayaz-Kala Desert Castles (Ellikqala, Karakalpakstan): Ancient Khwarazm
evidence.dateBasis: Painted clay-arch palace, Aramaic leather/wood archives & canal networks
evidence.summary: Rising above abandoned Amu Darya desert irrigation canals, Toprak-Kala's painted Hall of Kings and Ayaz-Kala's cliff citadels showcase pre-Islamic Afrighid Khwarazmian urban engineering.
evidence.limits: Desert wind erosion deeply flutes unbaked mudbrick tower faces.

evidence.title: Old Termez, Kara-Tepe & Fayaz-Tepe (Amu Darya Crossing, Uzbekistan): Kushan Buddhist Gate
evidence.dateBasis: Gandharan–Kushan limestone capitals, Brahmi/Kharosthi/Bactrian graffiti
evidence.summary: Guarding the strategic Oxus ferry between Bactria and Sogdia, Termez's cave-and-courtyard monasteries transmitted Indian Mahayana Buddhism, Greco-Kushan art, and cotton–rice farming northward.
evidence.limits: Riverbank fortification zones restrict public access in some peripheral sectors.

evidence.title: Kanka & Mingurik Citadels (Tashkent Oasis, Uzbekistan): Sogdian–Nomad Mint & Chach Border
evidence.dateBasis: Kangju–Chach bronze coins, multi-crop archaeobotany & kiln strata
evidence.summary: Bridging Syr Darya pastoral steppes and Sogdian agricultural oases, Chach/Shash minted distinctive ruler-and-tamgha copper coins and forged steel armor along the Silk Road's northern gate.
evidence.limits: Urban expansion in modern Tashkent overlaid much of medieval Binkent.

evidence.title: Shahrisabz Ak-Saray Palace & Bukhara Oasis Surveys (Uzbekistan): Timurid–Sogdian Heart
evidence.dateBasis: Glazed brick mosaic pylons (38 m) & Paykand–Bukhara oasis transects
evidence.summary: Birthplace of Timur, Shahrisabz's monumental mosaic portal and dense Bukharan canal survey grids chart how Timurid craftsmen from Shiraz, Damascus, and Khwarazm remade Central Asian oasis cities.
evidence.limits: 16th-century Abdullah Khan II wars demolished the Ak-Saray vault beyond its flanking pylons.

evidence.title: Jeitun Early Neolithic Mudbrick Village (Kopet Dag Piedmont, Turkmenistan): 6200 BCE Farming
evidence.dateBasis: AMS einkorn/barley grain dates & painted-floor mudbrick houses
evidence.summary: Single-room standardized mudbrick homes with red-ochre painted lime floors mark Jeitun as Central Asia's earliest confirmed village of domesticated wheat, barley, goat, and sheep herders.
evidence.limits: Small 0.7-hectare mound partially truncated by 1950s desert highway grading.

evidence.title: Gonur Depe Royal Citadel & Togolok 1 (Kara-Kum Delta, Turkmenistan): BMAC Oxus Capital
evidence.dateBasis: Polychrome wall paintings, royal chariot burials & archaeobotany
evidence.summary: Rising along an ancient Murghab River delta fan, Gonur Depe's fortified palace, water-temple basins, silver vessels, and Togolok grain stores anchor the Bronze Age Oxus Civilization.
evidence.limits: Shift of the Murghab delta westward forced site abandonment around 1500 BCE.

evidence.title: Old Nisa (Mithridatkert, Near Ashgabat, Turkmenistan): Royal Parthian Citadel & Ostraca
evidence.dateBasis: Ivory Hellenistic–Parthian rhytons & >2,700 Aramaic wine ostraca
evidence.summary: Fortified pentagonal citadel of early Arsacid Parthia housing columned round halls, carved ivory drinking horns, and thousands of vineyard-tax clay potsherds connecting Mediterranean art to steppe archers.
evidence.limits: Unbaked mudbrick walls eroded rapidly in seismic foothills after Sasanian conquest.

evidence.title: Anau North & Namazga-Depe Tells (Kopet Dag, Turkmenistan): Chalcolithic Copper–Wheat Towns
evidence.dateBasis: Multi-millennium tell stratigraphy & early arsenic-copper seals
evidence.summary: Deeply stratified Chalcolithic-to-Bronze Age tells along mountain-foot streams trace Central Asia's Indigenous shift from painted village ceramics to wheel-made vessels, metallurgy, and camel transport.
evidence.limits: Historic railway cuts exposed sections of Anau North prior to recent conservation.

evidence.title: Dehistan / Misrian Irrigated Plain (SW Turkmenistan): Medieval Atrek Caravan Metropolis
evidence.dateBasis: Canal levees, twin 20-m brick minarets & Khwarazmian pottery
evidence.summary: Sustained by 200 kilometers of engineered Atrek River canals across what is now arid clay desert, medieval Misrian linked Khorasan and Gorgan with Volga–Caspian trade before Mongol/climatic collapse.
evidence.limits: Desiccation of medieval canal intakes emptied the entire surrounding basin.

evidence.title: Sulaiman-Too Sacred Mountain & Bronze–Timurid Crossroads (Osh, Kyrgyzstan): Fergana Gate
evidence.dateBasis: Chust agrarian terrace houses, rock art & Babur Mosque sanctuary
evidence.summary: Five-peaked limestone ridge rising straight from the Fergana Valley, Sulaiman-Too anchors Bronze Age Chust sickle-farmer villages, Silk Road caravan shrines, and Babur's 1496 pavilion.
evidence.limits: Continuous pilgrimage construction modified earlier terrace shrines.

evidence.title: Tash Rabat 15th-Century Stone Caravanserai (At-Bashi, Naryn, 3,200 m, Kyrgyzstan): Tian Shan Pass
evidence.dateBasis: Half-subterranean slate masonry & 31 vaulted caravan chambers
evidence.summary: Built into a sheltered alpine valley below Torugart Pass between Kashgar and Lake Issyk-Kul, Tash Rabat's domed hall and stone stables sheltered winter silk, tea, and horse caravans from blizzards.
evidence.limits: Lacks foundation inscription; some archaeologists suggest earlier 10th-century monastic reuse.

evidence.title: Uzgen Karakhanid Mausolea & Minaret (Eastern Fergana, Kyrgyzstan): 11th–12th c. Bricks
evidence.dateBasis: Geometric baked-brick relief & Kufic–Persian architectural inscriptions
evidence.summary: Eastern capital of the Karakhanid state linking Balasagun and Kashgar across the Fergana Rim, Uzgen's three contiguous dynastic tombs showcase the summit of Central Asian sculpted terracotta brickwork.
evidence.limits: Upper minaret lantern collapsed in medieval earthquakes prior to 20th-century capping.

evidence.title: Saimaluu-Tash Alpine Petroglyphs (Fergana Range, 3,200 m, Kyrgyzstan): >90,000 Carvings
evidence.dateBasis: Glacial basalt moraine engravings of solar wheels, chariots & yaks
evidence.summary: Accessible only for six snow-free weeks each summer, Saimaluu-Tash preserves Central Asia's densest Bronze–Iron Age highland sanctuary linking pastoralists on both slopes of the Fergana Range.
evidence.limits: High-altitude frost shattering splinters fractured basalt boulders.

evidence.title: Sarazm Proto-Urban Settlement (Zarafshan Valley, Tajikistan): 3500–2000 BCE Tin & Wheat Hub
evidence.dateBasis: AMS wheat/barley grains, Baluchistan shell bangles & Afanasievo pottery
evidence.summary: Covering ~100 hectares where Zarafshan mountain passes meet Samarkand steppes, Sarazm traded local tin, turquoise, and gold for Makran shells and Turkmen ceramics centuries before the Silk Road.
evidence.limits: Excavations sample ~5% of the buried Chalcolithic–Early Bronze site.

evidence.title: Soii Havzak Stratified Loess Valley (Zeravshan, Tajikistan): New Inner Asian Paleolithic
evidence.dateBasis: Middle-to-Upper Paleolithic loess beds & Levallois-blade stratigraphy
evidence.summary: Newly excavated open-air paleosols in Tajikistan's Zeravshan Valley reveal repeated Middle and Upper Paleolithic human movements along the mountain piedmont linking Central Asia and Siberia.
evidence.limits: Final OSL chronology refinement across lower paleosols remains ongoing.

evidence.title: Ajina Tepe Buddhist Monastery (Vakhsh Valley, Tajikistan): 7th–8th c. Clay Nirvana Buddha
evidence.dateBasis: 13-meter painted clay *parinirvana* statue & Tocharian-era mural vaults
evidence.summary: Excavated in southern Tokharistan, Ajina Tepe's symmetrical mudbrick sanctuary preserves vivid wall paintings and monumental clay sculpture bridging Gandhara and Tang-era oasis art.
evidence.limits: Mudbrick walls eroded after eighth-century Arab conquest fires.

evidence.title: Yamchun Cliff Fortress & Wakhan Corridor Watchtowers (Gorno-Badakhshan, Tajikistan): Pamir Gate
evidence.dateBasis: Triangular stone-and-timber cliff bastions guarding the Panj–Oxus valley
evidence.summary: Perched high above the Panj River facing Afghanistan's Hindu Kush, Yamchun controlled high-altitude yak caravans linking Bactria, Gilgit-Kashmir, and Kashgar through the Wakhan Corridor.
evidence.limits: Few stratified organic deposits have been radiocarbon-tested inside outer ramparts.

evidence.title: Shortugai (Badakhshan) & Mundigak (Kandahar): 2200 BCE Harappan Lapis Outpost on the Oxus
evidence.dateBasis: Indus unicorn seals, etched carnelian beads & Badakhshan lapis flakes
evidence.summary: Located directly across the Kokcha River from Sar-e-Sang lapis lazuli mines, Shortugai operated an authentic Indus Valley irrigation colony exporting blue lapis to Harappa and Mesopotamia.
evidence.limits: Recent field surveys cannot revisit disturbed frontier riverbanks.

evidence.title: Ai-Khanoum (Oxus–Kokcha Confluence, Takhar, Afghanistan): 3rd–2nd c. BCE Greco-Bactrian Polis
evidence.dateBasis: Delphic Clearchus Greek maxims, Corinthian capitals & treasury ink dockets
evidence.summary: Containing a theater, gymnasium inscribed with Delphic proverbs, and Mesopotamian-style mudbrick temples, Ai-Khanoum fused Greek civic life with Central Asian irrigation until nomadic conquest ~145 BCE.
evidence.limits: Severe looting during late-20th-century wars scarred unexcavated lower town quarters.

evidence.title: Surkh Kotal Sanctuary & Balkh Bala Hisar (Northern Afghanistan): Kushan–Bactrian Capitals
evidence.dateBasis: Rabatak/Surkh Kotal Bactrian Greek-script steles & 10-km Balkh walls
evidence.summary: Monumental hillside stairs at Surkh Kotal and ancient Balkh (*Mother of Cities*) record Kanishka's Kushan Empire adopting Greek script for Iranian Bactrian language while bridging India, China, and Iran.
evidence.limits: Deep Hellenistic layers beneath Balkh lie under ten meters of Islamic mound overburden.

evidence.title: Bamiyan Cliff Buddhas & Monastic Cave Frescoes (Central Hindu Kush, Afghanistan): 4th–7th c.
evidence.dateBasis: Earliest oil-paint binder chemistry (walnut/poppy) & AMS soot dates
evidence.summary: Carved along the shortest caravan pass across the Hindu Kush between Balkh and Gandhara, Bamiyan's cliff caves preserve the world's oldest identified oil paintings (7th c. CE) beside Shahr-i-Gholghola.
evidence.limits: Dynamite destruction in 2001 pulverized the monumental 38-m and 55-m Buddha cores.

evidence.title: Herat Ikhtiyar al-Din Citadel & Gawhar Shad Musalla (Western Afghanistan): Timurid Renaissance
evidence.dateBasis: Glazed tilework minarets & 15th-century Herat scriptorium manuscripts
evidence.summary: Under Shah Rukh, Queen Gawhar Shad, and Ali-Shir Nava'i, 15th-century Herat flourished as the Persianate world's premier center of miniature painting, astronomy, Chagatai literature, and architectural tilework.
evidence.limits: 1885 military demolitions removed most of the Musalla except five surviving minarets.

evidence.title: Minaret of Jam / Firuzkuh (Hari Rud Canyon, Ghor, Afghanistan): 1194 CE Ghurid Brickwork
evidence.dateBasis: 65-meter baked-brick cylinder, Quranic Surah Maryam Kufic stucco
evidence.summary: Standing isolated inside a steep mountain canyon, the 1194 CE Minaret of Jam marks the lost Ghurid mountain capital of Firuzkuh along with Hebrew–Persian Jewish merchant cemeteries.
evidence.limits: Spring Hari Rud floods continuously undermine the octagonal brick plinth.

evidence.title: Lahuradewa & Koldihwa (Middle Ganga Plain, Uttar Pradesh): ~7000–6000 BCE Corded Rice
evidence.dateBasis: AMS charred rice phytoliths/grains & lake-core charcoal
evidence.summary: Lacustrine shore villages in the Sarayupar plain preserve cord-impressed pottery and cultivated *Oryza* grains documenting early Holocene Gangetic wetland rice trajectories.
evidence.limits: Debate continues between wild harvesting and early morphological domestication prior to 3000 BCE.

evidence.title: Barabar & Nagarjuni Mirror-Polished Granite Caves (Bihar): 3rd c. BCE Mauryan Architecture
evidence.dateBasis: Ashokan–Dasharatha Brahmi inscriptions & Lomas Rishi arched portal
evidence.summary: Chiseled into solid Archean granite hills by Emperor Ashoka for the Ajivika ascetics, Lomas Rishi's mirror-burnished rock vault inaugurates India's monumental rock-cut architectural tradition.
evidence.limits: Outer timber prototypes reflected in the carved facade do not survive anywhere.

evidence.title: Arikamedu (Puducherry) & Korkai (Tamil Nadu): Indo-Roman Amphora & Pearl-Fishery Ports
evidence.dateBasis: Arretine Terra Sigillata sherds, Roman amphorae & Indo-Pacific glass-bead kilns
evidence.summary: Paired Coromandel and Gulf of Mannar ports traded drawn glass beads, muslins, and Mannar pearls directly for Mediterranean wine amphorae and Roman gold-silver coin hoards.
evidence.limits: Coastal cyclone erosion and historical brick-quarrying disturbed upper port strata.

evidence.title: Vadnagar Deep Trench & Sharmishtha Tank (Northern Gujarat): 2,700-Year Continuous Citadel
evidence.dateBasis: 20-meter stratified mound, Buddhist vihara & conch-bangle workshops
evidence.summary: Continuously occupied through seven historical periods spanning pre-Mauryan ramparts, Buddhist monasteries, Kshatrapa coins, and Solanki toranas, Vadnagar illuminates Gujarat's overland link to Gulf ports.
evidence.limits: Deep water-table saturation limits broad horizontal exposure of pre-500 BCE levels.

evidence.title: Chittorgarh, Kumbhalgarh & Mehrangarh Hill Forts (Rajasthan): Rajput Ridge Architecture
evidence.dateBasis: 36-km Kumbhalgarh parapet wall, Victory Towers & rock-cut step-tanks
evidence.summary: Crowning steep Aravalli quartzite escarpments along Malwa–Gujarat caravan passes, Mewar and Marwar citadels integrated monsoon rainwater cisterns, palace courtyards, and kilometer-long stone battlements.
evidence.limits: Modern palace museum adaptations overlay interior residential wards.

evidence.title: Jaisalmer Golden Limestone Fort (Thar Desert, Rajasthan): 1156 CE Desert Silk Spur
evidence.dateBasis: Dry-interlocked Trikuta sandstone bastions & Jain library manuscripts
evidence.summary: Commanding desert wells between Sindh, Gujarat, and Delhi, Jaisalmer's living citadel protected Jain palm-leaf manuscript vaults and Paliwal camel caravans before maritime Bombay bypassed Thar tracks.
evidence.limits: Drainage seepage beneath limestone hilltops required emergency UNESCO conservation.

evidence.title: Belur Chennakeshava & Halebidu Hoysalesvara Temples (Karnataka): 12th c. Soapstone Craft
evidence.dateBasis: Lathe-turned chloritic schist pillars & stellate plinths
evidence.summary: Signed on their plinths by named master sculptors across the Mysore plateau, Hoysala stellate soapstone temples document guild patronage spanning overland bullock trade and Malabar spice duties.
evidence.limits: 14th-century Delhi Sultanate raids ended Halebidu's construction before gopurams were finished.

evidence.title: Leh Palace, Nubra Valley & Karakoram Pass Route (Ladakh, 3,500–5,540 m): Trans-Himalayan Gate
evidence.dateBasis: Namgyal timber-mud citadel, Rock-carved petroglyphs & Ladakh aDNA
evidence.summary: Bridging Kashmir, Tibet, and Yarkand across the world's highest caravan passes, Leh anchored Ladakh's wool (*pashmina*), salt, and Central Asian charas/jade exchange recorded in ancient regional genomes.
evidence.limits: High mountain trail shifting leaves few fixed caravanserai inns on the Karakoram plateau itself.

evidence.title: Kot Diji Citadel & Ranikot Wall (Khairpur–Jamshoro, Sindh): Pre-Harappan to Talpur Bastions
evidence.dateBasis: Stratified Kot Dijian ramparts & 32-km sandstone Kirthar hill-wall
evidence.summary: Kot Diji preserves fortified pre-Harappan stone bastions burnt just prior to Mature Indus integration, while Sindh's 32-kilometer Ranikot hill wall later enclosed desert passes west of the Indus.
evidence.limits: Ranikot's 19th-century Talpur rebuild obscures exact origins of its lower stone foundations.

evidence.title: Shah-ji-ki-Dheri (Peshawar) & Khyber Pass Forts (KP): Kushan Capital & Hindukush Hinge
evidence.dateBasis: Kanishka Reliquary Kharosthi inscription & Ali Masjid gorge bastions
evidence.summary: Anchor of Emperor Kanishka's winter capital Purushapura, Peshawar's stupa precinct and the winding Khyber gorge connected Gandharan Buddhist routes and caravans from Kabul down onto the Punjab plains.
evidence.limits: Urban brick harvesting dismantled the great Kanishka stupa superstructure before 1908 excavations.

evidence.title: Derawar Mudbrick Bastions & Cholistan Hakra Paleochannels (Punjab): Desert Frontier Forts
evidence.dateBasis: Dry Hakra-Ghaggar survey & 1733 CE Abbasi baked-brick circular towers
evidence.summary: Hundreds of unexcavated Hakra–Mature Harappan camps line the fossil Ghaggar-Hakra riverbed around Derawar's forty towering desert bastions guarding Multan–Jaisalmer camel tracks.
evidence.limits: Most Cholistan Hakra mounds remain mapped purely by surface sherd survey.

evidence.title: Baltit & Altit Timber-Stone Forts (Karimabad, Hunza, Karakoram): High-Mountain Pass Rule
evidence.dateBasis: Cribbed-juniper earthquake-resistant masonry & Kilik/Mintaka pass trails
evidence.summary: Guarding irrigated glacier-melt apricot terraces and steep Karakoram passes toward Wakhan and Yarkand, Baltit's juniper-tied stone watchtowers testify to Hunza Mir sovereignty into the 19th century.
evidence.limits: Frequent seismic repairs replaced exterior mud-plaster skins.

evidence.title: Lumbini Mayadevi Timber–Brick Shrine (Rupandehi Terai, Nepal): 6th c. BCE Stratified Pillar
evidence.dateBasis: OSL & AMS tree-shrine postholes beneath Ashoka's 249 BCE sandstone pillar
evidence.summary: Excavations beneath Ashoka's inscribed 249 BCE pillar uncovered sixth-century BCE postholes enclosing an open-air *bodhighara* tree shrine, providing earliest archaeological context for Buddhist origins.
evidence.limits: High monsoon water tables constrain deeper sub-trench expansions.

evidence.title: Gorkha Durbar Hill Palace & Ridge Fort (Gorkha, Central Nepal): 16th–18th c. Unification
evidence.dateBasis: Carved Newar-hill timber temple & Prithvi Narayan Shah campaign routes
evidence.summary: Crowning a knife-edge ridge along the Budhi Gandaki–Trisuli trade trails, the Shah kings launched the mid-18th-century campaigns from Gorkha that unified the Kathmandu Valley Malla cities into modern Nepal.
evidence.limits: 2015 Gorkha earthquake cracked perimeter walls prior to heritage masonry stabilization.

evidence.title: Rasuwa–Kyirong & Kuti–Kodari Trans-Himalayan Passes (Nepal–Tibet Border): Silver–Salt Artery
evidence.dateBasis: 17th–18th c. Malla coin treaties, stone bridges & custom-post ruins
evidence.summary: Through low gorge saddles cutting the Greater Himalaya at ~1,800–2,300 m, Kathmandu Newar merchants struck Tibet's silver *mahendramalli* coins and mediated Lhasa–Patna trade.
evidence.limits: Extreme monsoon landslides repeatedly erase stone trail switchbacks.

evidence.title: Simraungadh & Janakpurdham Ponds (Eastern Terai, Nepal): 11th–14th c. Karnata City
evidence.dateBasis: Fortified brick moat of Simraungadh & Maithili manuscript heritage
evidence.summary: Linking Ganga Valley trade from Bihar into Kathmandu before falling in 1325 CE, Simraungadh's brick citadel transmitted Maithili court drama, music, and Mithila artistic motifs directly to the Malla capitals.
evidence.limits: Simraungadh's forested brick ramparts remain minimally excavated.

evidence.title: Simtokha (1629) & Trongsa Dzong (1648, Central Bhutan): Unified Mountain-Pass Fortresses
evidence.dateBasis: Slate murals, *rammed-earth/stone* cantilever walls & pass registries
evidence.summary: Straddling the Mangde Chhu gorge where east–west trails funnel between central and western Bhutan, Trongsa and Simtokha paired monastic assemblies with administrative tax-and-defense citadels.
evidence.limits: Seismic fires in 1897 required faithful traditional timber reconstructions.

evidence.title: Drapham Dzong & Chummig Prehistory (Bumthang, Bhutan): Early Iron & Medieval Valley Excavations
evidence.dateBasis: Bhutan-Swiss AMS charcoal on fortress beams & early valley hearths
evidence.summary: Joint Bhutanese–Swiss excavations at Drapham Dzong documented layered 16th–17th century stone watchtowers alongside early Iron Age highland pastoralists moving between Tibet and Assam Duars.
evidence.limits: National archaeological heritage inventory remains in active early field stages.

evidence.title: Tremo La & Duar Foothill Trails (Haa–Chhukha, Bhutan): Silk–Rice–Dye Monsoon Corridors
evidence.dateBasis: Lhakhang Karpo/Nagpo valley trails & Phari–Koch Bihar trade records
evidence.summary: Steep mule paths through Haa and Chhukha carried Bengali endi silk, Assam lac dye, and rice up from the Duar foothills into Phari and Gyantse in exchange for Tibetan salt, wool, and musk.
evidence.limits: 19th-century Anglo-Bhutanese Duar conflicts altered southern foothill customs towns.

evidence.title: Bhitarghar Walled Frontier City (Panchagarh, Northern Bangladesh): 6th–12th c. Himalayan Gate
