evidence.dateBasis: Four-walled 25 sq km rampart moat & brick stupa foundations
evidence.summary: Covering twenty-five square kilometers along the Karatoya River corridor toward Sikkim and Tibet, Bhitarghar defended and taxed trans-Himalayan horse, musk, and cotton trade linking Kamarupa and Varendri.
evidence.limits: Modern village agriculture sits inside the outer earthen rampart rings.

evidence.title: Khalifatabad & Sixty Dome Mosque (Bagerhat, SW Bangladesh): 1459 CE Sundarbans City
evidence.dateBasis: Khan Jahan Ali terracotta brick domes & freshwater *dighi* reservoirs
evidence.summary: Carved out of tidal Sundarbans mangrove creeks with freshwater tank-reservoirs and curved *chala*-roofed terracotta mosques, Khalifatabad anchored 15th-century Bengal Delta reclamation and coastal shipping.
evidence.limits: Saline groundwater capillary rise necessitates periodic brick desalination.

evidence.title: Lalbagh Fort, Bara Katra & Buriganga Docks (Dhaka, Bangladesh): 17th c. Muslin Capital
evidence.dateBasis: Mughal water-channels, Subahdar garden vaults & river shipyard accounts
evidence.summary: Elevated by the Mughals as Jahangirnagar, Dhaka orchestrated the world's finest *jamdani* cotton-muslin weavers along the Meghna–Brahmaputra waterways and built war fleets against Arakanese corsairs.
evidence.limits: 1684 unfinished fort construction halted following Bibi Pari's death.

evidence.title: Chittagong / Chattagrama Harbor & Pandua Canal Docks (SE Bangladesh): Bay of Bengal Hub
evidence.dateBasis: Silver Harikela–Sultanate coin hoards & 16th c. *Porto Grande* logs
evidence.summary: From early Harikela silver-mint kingdoms to Bengal Sultanate and Arakan–Mughal rivalry, Chittagong served as the premier deep-water timber-shipbuilding and textile harbor of the eastern Bay of Bengal.
evidence.limits: Meandering Karnaphuli delta silt and 19th-century port dredging erased medieval quay trenches.

evidence.title: Mantai / Mahatittha Entrepôt (Mannar, NW Sri Lanka): 1st–11th c. Spice & Glass Hub
evidence.dateBasis: Charred Zanzibar/Maluku cloves, black pepper, Islamic glass & drone DEM
evidence.summary: Guarding the shallow Palk Strait passage, Mantai's twin moats yielded Roman-era carnelian, Sasanian turquoise jars, Changsha bowls, and some of the Indian Ocean's earliest charred clove and pepper grains.
evidence.limits: Silted channels cut off deep-draft vessel access after Chola–Polonnaruwa shifts.

evidence.title: Galle Harbor & Coral-Rampart Star Fort (SW Sri Lanka): Pre-Modern Cinnamon to Maritime Hinge
evidence.dateBasis: 1411 Zheng He trilingual stele, Portuguese seawalls & Dutch coral bastions
evidence.summary: Marked by Zheng He's 1411 trilingual Chinese–Tamil–Persian stele before Portuguese and Dutch coral-block ramparts rose above its natural bay, Galle exported highland cinnamon along the southern monsoon curve.
evidence.limits: Underwater shipwrecks outside Galle reefs preserve richer early cargoes than inland drains.

evidence.title: Yapahuwa Granite Citadel & Citadel Stairs (NW Sri Lanka): 13th c. Dry-Zone Transition
evidence.dateBasis: Lions-flanked carved granite staircase & Song–Yuan coin hoards
evidence.summary: Serving briefly as Sinhalese royal seat during Pandya invasions before capitals shifted wetter southwestward toward Kandy, Yapahuwa's ornamental cliff steps show South Indian–Khmer stylistic echoes.
evidence.limits: 1284 Pandya raid captured the Tooth Relic before abandonment.

evidence.title: Kuruhinna Tharaagandu (Kaashidhoo Atoll, Maldives): Pre-1153 CE Buddhist Coral Monasteries
evidence.dateBasis: Excavated *Porites* brain-coral stupas & 60,000+ stratified cowries
evidence.summary: Excavations across 64 carved brain-coral stupa cells and dense *Cypraea moneta* shell caches confirm thriving Dhivehi Buddhist maritime communities centuries prior to the 1153 CE conversion to Islam.
evidence.limits: Rising tides and limestone quarrying dismantled similar *havitta* mounds on southern atolls.

evidence.title: Malé Hukuru Miskiy Mosque & Atoll Cowrie Mint (Maldives): Indian Ocean Shell-Money Engine
evidence.dateBasis: Carved interlocking *Porites* coral ashlar & Bengal/West Africa cowrie ledgers
evidence.summary: Constructed without mortar from finely carved *Porites* brain-coral blocks, Malé's Friday Mosque stands at the heart of atolls whose *Cypraea moneta* cowries circulated as currency across Bengal, Yunnan, and West Africa.
evidence.limits: Colonial steam coinage and coastal reclamation curtailed large-scale cowrie dhow exports after 1850.

evidence.title: Con Moong & Xóm Trại Karst Caves (Thanh Hóa–Hòa Bình, Vietnam): Hoabinhian–Bacsonian
evidence.dateBasis: Stratified river-cobble *sumatraliths*, shell middens & edge-ground axes
evidence.summary: Deep karst cave deposits record Pleistocene-to-Holocene transitions from flaked river-pebble choppers to Bacsonian edge-ground stone axes, bamboo exploitation, and cord-marked woodland pots.
evidence.limits: Tropical limestone karst percolation disrupts minor charcoal flecks.

evidence.title: Hội An (Faifo) Ancient Port & Cù Lao Chàm Wreck (Quảng Nam, Vietnam): 15th–18th c. Trade
evidence.dateBasis: Chu Đậu blue-and-white wreck cargo, Japanese Bridge & Fujian guildhalls
evidence.summary: Along the Thu Bồn Estuary, Red Seal Japanese ships (*shuinsen*), Fujian merchant junks, and Chu Đậu kiln cargos made Hội An Southeast Asia's premier 16th–17th century ceramic, silk, and eaglewood emporium.
evidence.limits: River siltation shifted deep-draft European steam shipping north to Đà Nẵng by 1850.

evidence.title: Trà Kiệu (Simhapura) & Chà Bàn (Vijaya) Brick Capitals (Central Vietnam): Champa Heartland
evidence.dateBasis: Sanskrit Vo Canh–Tra Kieu steles, brick towers & Cham glazed kilns
evidence.summary: Anchoring Champa's coastal river-valleys, Trà Kiệu and Vijaya minted Sanskrit inscriptions, fielded outrigger fleets across the South China Sea, and fired Champa-style greenwares at Gò Sành.
evidence.limits: 20th-century wars severely scarred surface brick tower complexes around Vijaya.

evidence.title: Citadel of the Hồ Dynasty (Tây Đô, Thanh Hóa, Vietnam): 1397 CE Cyclopean Limestone Walls
evidence.dateBasis: Dry-fitted 20-ton limestone blocks & arched stone gates
evidence.summary: Constructed in 1397 in one year along the Mã River using interlocking 10-to-26-ton carved limestone blocks without mortar, the Hồ Citadel reflects late Trần–Hồ Đại Việt administrative reform and stone-vault engineering.
evidence.limits: Only perimeter stone walls and four arched gates survived 15th-century conflict.

evidence.title: An Sơn & Giồng Cá Vồ (Southern Vietnam): Neolithic Rice & Nephrite Double-Headed Ear Ornaments
evidence.dateBasis: Domesticated rice phytoliths, domestic pigs & Taiwan *lingling-o* nephrite
evidence.summary: Southern Vietnamese mound-villages and coastal mangrove jar cemeteries reveal early Mekong rice cultivation transitioning directly into the South China Sea Taiwan-to-Palawan Fengtien jade-ring network.
evidence.limits: Acidic coastal mangrove alluvium limits uncremated bone survival at Giồng Cá Vồ.

evidence.title: Spirit Cave (Mae Hong Son) & Moh Khiew Cave (Krabi, Thailand): Hoabinhian Forest-Coast
evidence.dateBasis: AMS bone/charcoal dates, bamboo-processing lithics & extended burials
evidence.summary: From highland Shan karst shelters in northern Thailand to limestone cliffs in Krabi, Hoabinhian foragers mastered tropical plant-tuber processing, bamboo tools, and flexed burials across 20 millennia.
evidence.limits: Early 1970s Spirit Cave plant-domestication claims were revised downward to wild foraging.

evidence.title: U Thong & Nakhon Pathom (Chao Phraya Basin, Thailand): 6th–11th c. Dvaravati Mon Towns
evidence.dateBasis: Pali *Ye Dhamma* brick steles, moats & tin-silver rising-sun coins
evidence.summary: Set along ancient tidal Chao Phraya shorelines, moated Dvaravati Mon cities minted standardized silver coins, carved sandstone Dharmachakra wheels, and traded Roman-style seals across coastal Siam.
evidence.limits: Deltaic river shifts displaced shoreline ports seaward away from U Thong.

evidence.title: Chiang Saen (Mekong) & Chiang Mai Walled Capital (Lanna, N. Thailand): Caravan Crossroads
evidence.dateBasis: Brick *chedi* temples, Kalong celadon kilns & Lanna–Yunnan horse trails
evidence.summary: Founded in 1296 by King Mangrai, Lanna's Chiang Mai and Chiang Saen channeled Yunnanese Hui caravans, Shan lacquerers, and Ping River rice barges across the Shan–Mekong hill crossroads.
evidence.limits: 16th–18th century Burmese suzerainty altered older wooden palace compounds.

evidence.title: Chaiya, Satingphra & Takuapa (Isthmus of Kra, Southern Thailand): Trans-Peninsular Portages
evidence.dateBasis: Tang Changsha bowls, Middle Eastern turquoise glass & Srivijayan inscriptions
evidence.summary: Narrow overland river-and-elephant portages across the Isthmus of Kra allowed merchants to bypass Malacca piracy, depositing Middle Eastern turquoise-glazed jars beside Tang celadon and Pallava statues.
evidence.limits: Tin-dredging and rubber planting disturbed alluvial port trenches at Takuapa.

evidence.title: Khao Wong Prachan & Lopburi / Lavo (Central Thailand): 2nd Mill. BCE Copper Smelters
evidence.dateBasis: Industrial crucible-slag mounds & Prang Sam Yot Khmer–Ayutthaya forts
evidence.summary: Smelting hills in the Khao Wong Prachan valley cast millions of copper-alloy ingots shipped down the Chao Phraya 1,500 years before historic Lavo became an Angkorian–Ayutthayan royal hub.
evidence.limits: Slag quarrying for modern road aggregate damaged peripheral Non Pa Wai hills.

evidence.title: Tham Hang & Viengxay Karst Caves (Houaphanh, NE Laos): Pleistocene–Hoabinhian Passages
evidence.dateBasis: Karst sediment C14 & Hoabinhian edge-ground adzes
evidence.summary: High limestone passes between northern Laos and Vietnam's Mã River preserve terminal Pleistocene hunter-gatherer rock shelters bridging mountain valleys with Tonkin coastal groups.
evidence.limits: 1960s–70s war bunkers altered upper floor levels at Viengxay caverns.

evidence.title: Vientiane Pha That Luang & Xieng Khouang Stupas (Mekong Valley, Laos): Lan Xang Seat
evidence.dateBasis: Brick-and-gilt 1566 pyramid stupa & sandstone Buddha inscriptions
evidence.summary: Moving Lan Xang's administrative capital downstream from Luang Prabang to Vientiane in 1560 under King Setthathirath integrated middle Mekong rice plains, benzoin resin, and Lao monastic scholarship.
evidence.limits: 1827–1828 Siamese razing destroyed most wooden Vientiane temples except Wat Sisaket.

evidence.title: Vilabouly (Sepon) Ancient Copper Mines (Savannakhet, Laos): 1000 BCE–300 CE Timber Shafts
evidence.dateBasis: Waterlogged rattan baskets, ladders, crucibles & lead-isotope match
evidence.summary: Deep wooden mine shafts preserved beneath wet malachite ore yielded intact rattan ore baskets and smelting crucibles whose lead isotopes match Bronze Age drums across Vietnam and Thailand.
evidence.limits: Uncovered during modern open-pit mining operations; continuous rescue monitoring continues.

evidence.title: Laang Spean Stratified Cave (Battambang, NW Cambodia): 71 ka–1000 BCE Occupation
evidence.dateBasis: OSL-dated Hoabinhian choppers & ~3300 BP Neolithic flexed burials
evidence.summary: Set inside a Permian limestone hill overlooking the Sangker plain, Laang Spean preserves one of Mainland Southeast Asia's longest stratified records from pre-50 ka tools through Hoabinhian hunters and Neolithic potters.
evidence.limits: Sub-meter sterile carbonate crusts separate earlier Pleistocene layers.

evidence.title: Angkor Borei & Phnom Da Brick-Canal Metropolis (Takéo, Cambodia): Inland Twin of Óc Eo
evidence.dateBasis: Kilometer-long Funan barge canals, Vat Komnou burials & 6th c. Vishnu sculpture
evidence.summary: Linked directly to the coastal port of Óc Eo via an engineered 70-kilometer straight canal across the Mekong floodplain, walled Angkor Borei reveals Funan's dense brick urbanism and Sanskrit–Khmer state origins.
evidence.limits: Annual Mekong floods deposit thick clay across non-mounded residential quarters.

evidence.title: Phnom Kulen (Mahendraparvata, Siem Reap, Cambodia): 802 CE Sacred Mountain & Quarries
evidence.dateBasis: LiDAR orthogonal gridded city, earthen reservoirs & riverbed Shiva lingas
evidence.summary: Airborne LiDAR beneath dense forest revealed Mahendraparvata's 802 CE rectilinear avenues, earthen check-dams, and sandstone quarries that supplied the temple-blocks floated downriver to Angkor.
evidence.limits: Thick Dipterocarp jungle canopy and historic unexploded ordnance restrict wide hand-trenching.

evidence.title: Lovek & Udōng River Capitals (Kampong Chhnang–Kandal, Cambodia): 1528–1866 Maritime Shift
evidence.dateBasis: Tonle Sap moats, Japanese–Portuguese trade deeds & royal chedi stupas
evidence.summary: Shifting downriver from Angkor toward the Tonle Sap–Mekong junction, Lovek and Udōng hosted Japanese *shuinsen* traders, Dutch factors, and Theravada *vihear* halls integrated into South China Sea shipping.
evidence.limits: 1594 and 18th-century regional wars damaged brick palace citadels.

evidence.title: Padah-Lin Karst Shelters (Shan Plateau, Myanmar): Paleolithic–Neolithic Cave Art & Cordware
evidence.dateBasis: Charcoal radiocarbon on pebble-tool hearths & red-ochre cattle/hand murals
evidence.summary: Red-ochre bulls, fish, sunrise discs, and human hands overlooking western Shan hills mark Upper Paleolithic-to-Hoabinhian edge-ground toolmakers linking Myanmar's Irrawaddy uplands to Thailand and Yunnan.
evidence.limits: Pigment panels remain anchored indirectly by associated hearth radiocarbon dates.

evidence.title: Martaban (Mottama), Twante & Bago Kiln Ports (Lower Myanmar): Ocean Martaban Storage Jars
evidence.dateBasis: Dragon kilns, black-brown glazed *martaban* water jars & Mon annals
evidence.summary: Heavy salt-and-ash-glazed stoneware jars fired around Martaban and Twante became the standard freshwater and spice-storage containers aboard ships from the Red Sea to Japan's tea houses.
evidence.limits: Mon–Burmese campaigns in the 18th century dismantled Bago's wooden docks.

evidence.title: Innwa (Ava) Citadel & Mandalay Royal Teak Palace (Irrawaddy, Myanmar): 1364–1885 Capitals
evidence.dateBasis: Inscribed Kuthodaw 729-marble Pali Tripitaka & brick river forts
evidence.summary: Controlling the Myitnge–Irrawaddy confluence and northern jade–rubies–cotton caravans into Yunnan, Ava, Amarapura, and Mandalay produced monumental teak monasteries and the world's largest stone-carved Tripitaka.
evidence.limits: 1839 earthquake and 1945 bombing destroyed Mandalay's original wooden palace except brick moats.

evidence.title: Tenasserim (Tanintharyi) & Mergui Harbor (Southern Myanmar): Isthmus Trade to Siam
evidence.dateBasis: Sukhothai/Ming-ceramic finds along the Little Tenasserim pass to Ayutthaya
evidence.summary: Serving as Ayutthaya's Indian Ocean port on the Andaman flank, Mergui and Tenasserim funneled Coromandel textiles, tin, and sappanwood overland across the Tenasserim Range to the Gulf of Thailand.
evidence.limits: Dense rainforest trails across the Tenasserim pass retain few standing stone waystations.

evidence.title: Lenggong Valley (Kota Tampan, Bukit Bunuh & Gua Gunung Runtuh, Perak): 1.83 Ma to Perak Man
evidence.dateBasis: 74 ka Youngest Toba Tuff ash bed & ~10.1 ka AMS Perak Man skeleton
evidence.summary: Paleolithic stone-knapping floors sandwiched directly inside 74,000-year-old Toba volcanic ash and the 10,120-year-old congenital-limb skeleton of Perak Man make Lenggong a cornerstone of Malay Peninsula prehistory.
evidence.limits: Fission-track dates >1.8 Ma on impact-suevite handaxes at Bukit Bunuh remain debated.

evidence.title: Guar Kepah Shell Midden (Penang) & Gua Cha (Kelantan, Malaysia): Hoabinhian–Neolithic Sequence
evidence.dateBasis: AMS shell dates, tripod corded pottery & Hoabinhian–Malayo-Polynesian skeletons
evidence.summary: Comparing inland Gua Cha limestone-cave flexed burials with Guar Kepah's coastal mangrove cockle middens reveals cultural coexistence and transition between mainland Hoabinhian foragers and Neolithic farmers.
evidence.limits: 19th-century lime-burning quarried away large sections of the Guar Kepah shell mounds.

evidence.title: Kuala Selinsing Mangrove Stilt-Settlement (Perak, Malaysia): 200 BCE–1000 CE Bead Port
evidence.dateBasis: Dugout watercraft, Pallava carnelian seal & coastal tin-glass beads
evidence.summary: Built on stilts amid tidal Perak mangroves, Kuala Selinsing's shell-midden islanders manufactured gold ornaments, glass and agate beads, and outrigger hulls feeding the Bujang Valley–Srivijaya network.
evidence.limits: Rising mangrove siltation reworks submerged house-post horizons.

evidence.title: Santubong Delta Iron-Smelting Complexes (Kuching, Sarawak, Borneo): 10th–14th c. Steel Hub
evidence.dateBasis: Tens of thousands of tons of iron slag, clay tuyeres & Tang–Song celadons
evidence.summary: Beneath Mount Santubong, Bornean smelters converted coastal laterite ore into crucible steel ingots traded directly for Longquan greenwares, Dehua porcelain, camphor, and hornbill ivory.
evidence.limits: Tropical humidity decayed wooden riverside wharves next to enduring iron slag mounds.

evidence.title: Song Terus & Braholo Caves (Gunung Sewu Karst, East Java): 40–5 ka Tool–Bone Sequence
evidence.dateBasis: AMS flexed skeletons, Sampung bone spatulas & fluvial flake tools
evidence.summary: Spanning deep Pleistocene chert flakes through Sampung early Holocene bone-point artisans and Austronesian-era burials, Gunung Sewu caves document continuous technological resilience on southern Java.
evidence.limits: Karst tectonic uplift and sinkhole slumping compact earliest alluvial horizons.

evidence.title: Buni Culture Necropoles & Batujaya Brick Stupas (Karawang, West Java): 200 BCE–600 CE
evidence.dateBasis: Tarumanagara brick temple *Blandongan*, Indian rouletted ware & gold ornaments
evidence.summary: Rising above paddies along West Java's northern delta, Buni stamped-pottery graves with Indian rouletted ceramics underlie Batujaya's Tarumanagara brick stupas—among Indonesia's earliest monumental Buddhist shrines.
evidence.limits: Subsurface clay moisture threatens low-fired rice-husk-tempered bricks once exposed.

evidence.title: Riau–Lingga Archipelago Coastal Shelters & Shipwreck Littoral (Sumatra–Singapore Strait)
evidence.dateBasis: Geological sea-level shelf mapping & Riau-Lingga Bugis–Malay sultanate sites
evidence.summary: Positioned at the submerged Sunda Shelf bottleneck where all China-to-India shipping funnels, Riau–Lingga's *Orang Laut* sea peoples piloted royal Srivijayan, Melakan, and Johor-Riau fleets.
evidence.limits: Post-glacial sea-level rise drowned Pleistocene Sunda river valleys across the strait.

evidence.title: Somba Opu Brick Citadel (Gowa–Makassar, South Sulawesi): 16th–17th c. Spice-Trepang Hub
evidence.dateBasis: 3-meter brick bastions, *Lontara* chronicle archives & global spice cargos
evidence.summary: Operating a free-trade port welcoming Malay, Portuguese, Chinese, and English vessels in defiance of Dutch monopoly claims, Makassar linked Maluku cloves directly to Java, Manila, and Australian Arnhem Land.
evidence.limits: Razed after the 1669 Treaty of Bungaya and exposed only during late-20th-century river dredging.

evidence.title: Banda Islands (Banda Neira, Lontor & Run, Maluku): Global Nutmeg–Mace Epicenter
evidence.dateBasis: 4,000-year Ay obsidian/pottery, Javanese-Chinese sherds & VOC nutmeg *perken*
evidence.summary: For centuries the world's sole source of nutmeg and mace, Banda's volcanic coral-walled settlements exchanged spices via Javanese and Makassarese junks long before the 1621 Dutch conquest and Run–Manhattan swap.
evidence.limits: 1621 colonial depopulation severed continuous indigenous village oral lineages on central Banda.

evidence.title: Samudra Pasai & Aceh Darussalam (Northern Sumatra): Earliest Indonesian Sultanate & Pepper Port
evidence.dateBasis: 1297 Sultan Malik al-Saleh tombstone, *dirham* gold coins & Ottoman-pepper ties
evidence.summary: Anchoring the northern gateway of the Malacca Strait where Indian Ocean monsoon vessels first sighted landfall, Pasai and Aceh minted Islamic gold *mas* coins and exported Sumatran black pepper.
evidence.limits: 2004 Indian Ocean tsunami reshaped low-lying coastal cemetery zones around Banda Aceh.

evidence.title: Ille Cave & Dewil Valley (El Nido, Northern Palawan, Philippines): 14 ka Terminal Foragers
evidence.dateBasis: AMS 9,000 BP human cremation burial & shell bead assemblages
evidence.summary: Preserving Southeast Asia's earliest documented secondary human cremation (~7000 BCE) alongside cut-and-drilled shell beads and deer bones, Ille Cave reveals shrinking Sunda-shelf coastlines in northern Palawan.
evidence.limits: Monsoon bat guano acidifies deeper Pleistocene bone lenses.

evidence.title: Bubog I & II Rock Shelters (Ilin Island, Mindoro, Philippines): 33–4 ka Maritime Foragers
evidence.dateBasis: Calibrated marine-shell *Geloina* tools, obsidian & pelagic fishbone
evidence.summary: Facing deep-water Mindoro Strait crossings since 33,000 years ago, Bubog foragers flaked giant mangrove-clam shell adzes (~7,500 cal BP) and transferred exotic obsidian across Philippine channels.
evidence.limits: Shell middens require local marine-reservoir calibration adjustments.

evidence.title: Savidug Ijang Hillforts & Sunget (Batanes Islands, Luzon Strait): Austronesian Stepping Stones
evidence.dateBasis: Taiwan Fengtien nephrite cores, stone-walled terraced *ijang* citadels
evidence.summary: Linking eastern Taiwan across treacherous Luzon Strait currents, Batanes sites yield red-slipped Austronesian pottery (~4000 BP), worked Taiwan jade, boat-shaped burials, and stone-stepped *ijang* fortified hilltops.
evidence.limits: Severe seasonal typhoons strip shallow ridge-top loam outside ditched *ijang* mounds.

evidence.title: Cebu Sugbo Harbor & Rajahnate Precinct (Visayas, Philippines): Ming Celadon–Gold Hub
evidence.dateBasis: Excavated Song–Ming blue-and-white grave porcelains, gold filigree & iron slag
evidence.summary: Positioned at the crossroads of the Visayan archipelago before Legazpi's 1565 landing, Sugbo's waterfront yielded thousands of Song–Ming trade ceramics traded for cotton textiles, beeswax, and Visayan goldwork.
evidence.limits: Urban port expansion in Cebu City covers medieval shoreline middens.

evidence.title: Jolo Harbor & Sulu Archipelago Maritime Network (Southern Philippines): Pearl & Camphor Sultanate
evidence.dateBasis: Royal coral-stone *astana* genealogy tombs & Canton-Manila junk manifests
evidence.summary: Bridging Borneo, Mindanao, and Maluku seas, the Sulu Sultanate dispatched *panco* and *lanong* fleets supplying Canton markets with Sulu pearls, bird's nests, camphor, and trepang into the 19th century.
evidence.limits: 1876 and late-19th-century naval bombardments destroyed timber dock structures at Jolo.

evidence.title: Kota Batu Archaeological Park (Brunei River): 14th–17th c. Sultanate Stone Rampart & Port
evidence.dateBasis: 2.5-km dry-stone causeways, Ming blue-and-white sherds & tomb steles
evidence.summary: Named after its stone seawalls and carved royal tombstones, Kota Batu connected the Sultanate of Brunei's dry-camphor and pearl interior with Ming treasure fleets, Melaka, and Manila.
evidence.limits: Tidal swamps waterlog wooden piling alongside stone quay alignments.

evidence.title: Sungai Limau Manis (10th–13th c.) & Kampong Ayer Water Metropolis (Brunei): Stilt Urbanism
evidence.dateBasis: 50,000+ Song–Yuan ceramic sherds, timber house posts & bronze cannons
evidence.summary: From Sungai Limau Manis's dense Song–Yuan river emporium to historic Kampong Ayer's timber walkways spanning Brunei Bay, Bornean water towns integrated river trade directly from household boat landings.
evidence.limits: Continuous timber house rebuilding obscures earlier 15th–16th century stilt plans.

evidence.title: Fort Canning Hill (Bukit Larangan) & Empress Place (Singapore): 14th c. Temasek Seat
evidence.dateBasis: Yuan *shufu* blue-and-white compass bowls, Javanese gold & glass bangle waste
evidence.summary: Stratified excavations on Fort Canning and the Singapore River banks uncovered glass-recycling workshops, Song–Yuan coins, and high-grade Yuan porcelains confirming Temasek as a cosmopolitan 14th-century emporium.
evidence.limits: 19th-century British hill leveling truncated palace terraces near the summit.

evidence.title: Singapore River Godowns & Keppel Deep-Water Straits (Singapore): 1819–1900 Free-Port Hinge
evidence.dateBasis: Harbor reclamation charts, Chinese–Bugis *twakow* logs & Straits customs
evidence.summary: Replacing older estuarine quays with a duty-free entrepôt linking Malacca tin, Javanese coffee, Sarawak gambier, and Chinese steam-era migration, Singapore transformed Southeast Asian shipping.
evidence.limits: 20th-century dockland towers cover 1820s timber *attap* boatyards.

evidence.title: Matja Kuru 1 & 2 Caves (Lake Ira Lalaro, Lautém, Timor-Leste): 32 ka Uplands & ~3000 BP Dog
evidence.dateBasis: AMS radiocarbon on charcoal, cuscus bones & 3000 BP domestic dog burial
evidence.summary: Overlooking Timor-Leste's largest freshwater highland lake, Matja Kuru bridges Pleistocene upland foraging with Neolithic ~3,000-year-old dog burials and red-slipped Austronesian ceramics.
evidence.limits: Reworked karst cave dust mixes shallow Neolithic pits into older Pleistocene units.

evidence.title: Ili Kéré-Kéré Painted Cliffs & Oecusse Sandalwood Coast (Timor-Leste): Maritime Exchange
evidence.dateBasis: Austronesian *Oliva* shell beads, boat motifs & sandalwood port deeds
evidence.summary: Polychrome cliff paintings of outrigger craft at Ili Kéré-Kéré and Topass–Chinese–Malay sandalwood harbors along Oecusse link Timor's fragrant white sandalwood forests to Canton and Macau markets.
evidence.limits: Salt-spray weathering fades cliff pigments outside sheltered limestone overhangs.

evidence.title: Pskov Krom & Izborsk Limestone Citadels (NW Russia): 862–1700 Western Frontier Bastion
evidence.dateBasis: Truvor Mound stratigraphy, Devonian limestone curtains & 1581 siege chronicles
evidence.summary: Guarding Rus's western Baltic approaches alongside Veliky Novgorod, Pskov's triple concentric stone curtains and Izborsk Plateau fortress channeled Hanseatic wax, flax, and Siberian fur routes.
evidence.limits: 17th-century earthen bastions added by Peter I overbuilt older outer timber towers.

evidence.title: Rostov Veliky Kremlin & Yaroslavl Upper Volga Entrepôt: 9th–18th c. Orthodox Heartland
evidence.dateBasis: Timerëvo Scandinavian-Slavic mound cemetery & 17th c. frescoed Volga churches
evidence.summary: Anchored by the Viking-age Timber-and-Dirham trading cemetery at Timerëvo near Yaroslavl and Rostov's lake-bordered kremlin, Upper Volga towns fused Baltic trade with Muscovite polychrome church art.
evidence.limits: Early 10th-century wooden town houses lie beneath modern Rostov streets.

evidence.title: Tula Kremlin & Great Abatis Line (Zasechnaya Cherta, Oka Basin): 16th c. Steppe Defense Wall
evidence.dateBasis: 600-km felled-oak forest barrier, Tula brick fort & 1632 iron armories
evidence.summary: Combining felled-forest *zaseka* entanglements with earthen ramparts and stone kremlins like Tula across southern Rus, Muscovy's Forest-Steppe Line blunted Crimean raids and enabled Ural–Siberian ironworks.
evidence.limits: Timber forest-strip boundaries disappeared as southern chernozem prairies were ploughed.

evidence.title: Obdorsk / Polui Promontory Fair (Salekhard, Lower Ob, 66.5°N): Subarctic Fur & Khanty Sanctuary
evidence.dateBasis: Subarctic permafrost timber stockade & Nenets–Khanty–Russian winter fair records
evidence.summary: Set right on the Arctic Circle at the mouth of the Polui into the Ob, Obdorsk grew alongside ancient permafrost sanctuaries into the northernmost winter trading fair exchanging reindeer hides and polar fox for grain and brass.
evidence.limits: Continuous permafrost heave twisted original 16th-century log footings.

evidence.title: Iturup & Shumshu Sea-Mammal Sites (Kuril Archipelago, Russian Far East): North Pacific Arc
evidence.dateBasis: Tephra-dated pit-houses, Okhotsk sea-lion middens & obsidian provenance
evidence.summary: Volcanic stepping stones between Hokkaido and Kamchatka preserve subterranean Jōmon, Epi-Jōmon, Okhotsk, and Kuril Ainu villages connected by Hokkaido obsidian and sea-otter trade long before Imperial border treaties.
evidence.limits: Earthquakes, tsunamis, and tephrochronology complicate narrow shallow middens.

evidence.title: Jiumenkou Nine-Gate River Great Wall (Suizhong, Liaoning): Hydraulic Arched Wall Bridge
evidence.dateBasis: Nine granite sluice arches spanning the Jiujiang River valley
evidence.summary: Instead of ending at the riverbank, Ming engineers built the only Great Wall segment bridging directly across a river valley via nine arched sluice-gates fortified with defensive iron portcullises.
evidence.limits: Heavy summer flash floods washed away original iron river grilles prior to 1980s restoration.

evidence.title: Xuanquanzhi Han Courier Relay Station (Guazhou–Dunhuang, Gansu): 23,000 Bamboo Slips
evidence.dateBasis: 23,000+ ink-inscribed wood/bamboo slips, wall decrees & horse rations
evidence.summary: Excavated halfway along the arid Hexi corridor between Dunhuang and Anxi, this walled courtyard post-station preserves daily guest registries of Kangju, Kushan, Khotan, and Han ambassadors dining beside relay stables.
evidence.limits: Arid deflation exposed southern courtyard rubbish middens prior to shelter roofing.

evidence.title: Fuzhou Three Lanes–Seven Alleys & Pagoda Anchorage Shipyard (Fujian): Min Maritime Nexus
evidence.dateBasis: Tang–Qing timber ward plan, Ryukyu guest mission & 1866 Arsenal docks
evidence.summary: Hosting the official Ryukyu Kingdom guesthouse and exporting Wuyi bohea black tea from inland rivers down the Min Estuary, Fuzhou later launched China's first modern steam dockyard in 1866.
evidence.limits: 19th-century tea godowns along Nantai docks were rebuilt after colonial treaty-port fires.

evidence.title: Xining Beichan Caves & Huangshui Valley (Qinghai): Tang–Tibetan–Sogdian Tea Border
evidence.dateBasis: Sasanian–Byzantine coin grave finds, Han ramparts & Amdo horse fairs
evidence.summary: Commanding the Huangshui Corridor between Lanzhou and Kokonor (Qinghai Lake), Xining yielded Sasanian silver drachms and anchored Sino–Tibetan horse-for-tea exchanges across Amdo.
evidence.limits: Modern industrial expansion covers peripheral Han–Tang military farm trenches.

evidence.title: Gwalior Gopachal Hill Fort & Teli ka Mandir (Madhya Pradesh): 6th–16th c. Gateway of Hind
evidence.dateBasis: Zero numeral inscription (876 CE Chaturbhuj Temple) & Man Mandir glazed tiles
evidence.summary: Controlling the Chambal trunk corridor linking Delhi and Agra to the Deccan, Gwalior's sandstone cliff citadel preserves one of India's earliest dated epigraphic decimal zero inscriptions (876 CE) and Tomar glazed-tile walls.
evidence.limits: Successive Kachwaha, Tomar, Suri, Mughal, and Scindia garrisons reworked interior palaces.

evidence.title: Kalimpong–Jelep La Ridge & Tumlong–Rabdentse (Sikkim–Bengal): Youngest Himalaya Wool Road
evidence.dateBasis: Rabdentse 17th c. stone ruins & Jelep La wool-caravan customs counts
evidence.summary: Bridging Lhasa and Gyantse over 4,267-meter Jelep La directly down to Bengal railheads via Kalimpong, Sikkim's Namgyal ridge capitals channeled half of all Tibetan wool exports by 1900.
evidence.limits: Dense cloud-forest moss and monsoon slips erode unmortared Rabdentse ruin terraces.

evidence.title: Ternate (Gamlamo) & Tidore Coral-Stone Sultanate Forts (North Maluku): Endemic Clove Twin Hubs
evidence.dateBasis: Sultanate stone citadels, Ming ceramics & clove monopoly treaties
evidence.summary: Until 18th-century smuggling, endemic *Syzygium aromaticum* clove trees grew solely on five tiny volcanic cones around Ternate and Tidore, funding rival Maluku Islamic sultanates whose fleets reached Papua and Java.
evidence.limits: Portuguese, Spanish, and Dutch coastal bastions overbuilt earlier wooden *kraton* compounds.

evidence.title: Övgön Khiid & Shankh Khüree Monasteries (Övörkhangai–Bulgan): Khalkha Scriptoriums
evidence.dateBasis: Khögno Khan mountain masonry & Zanabazar nomadic temple remnants
evidence.summary: Built along Khögno Khan's sheltered granite valleys north of Karakorum, Khalkha monastic scriptoriums safeguarded Tibetan-Mongolian medicinal texts, brass-gilt sculpture ateliers, and steppe postal staging.
evidence.limits: 17th-century Oirat–Khalkha conflicts and 1930s closures damaged early chapels.

evidence.title: Byokrando International Estuary Port & Kaesong Fortress (Hwanghae): Goryeo Arabian Ties
evidence.dateBasis: Yesong River tidal docks, Arab merchant records & Goryeo celadon cargos
evidence.summary: Positioned at the Yesong River mouth serving Goryeo's capital Kaesong, Byokrando welcomed Song Chinese, Jurchen, Japanese, and Arab merchants importing mercury and spice for Korean ginseng and celadon.
evidence.limits: Riverine sedimentation and DMZ estuary borders prevent modern open excavation of Byokrando.

evidence.title: Tongdosa (Yangsan, 646 CE) & Songgwangsa Sanbo Monasteries (Korea): Three-Jewel Hubs
evidence.dateBasis: Silla–Joseon carved stone ordination stupa, bell & woodblock archives
evidence.summary: Founded during Silla's Tang exchange and rebuilt across Goryeo and Joseon centuries, Korea's Three-Jewel mountain monasteries anchored Seon meditation, temple-woodblock publishing, and artisan guilds.
evidence.limits: Wooden pavilion halls underwent post-1592 Joseon rebuilds above Silla–Goryeo stone foundations.

evidence.title: Nagoya Castle Stone Bastions & Owari Tokugawa Axis (Aichi, 1612): Shinpan Citadel
evidence.dateBasis: Ieyasu-ordered Honmaru Palace cypress woodwork & stone-mason signatures
evidence.summary: Built by twenty Allied daimyō lords under Tokugawa Ieyasu's direct order to anchor the Tōkaidō–Nakasendō corridor against Toyotomi Osaka, Nagoya's massive stone walls bear daimyō mason quarry marks.
evidence.limits: Main 1612 wooden keep and Honmaru palace burned in 1945 bombing (Honmaru meticulously rebuilt in cypress).

evidence.title: Hagi Castle Town & Shōkasonjuku Academy (Yamaguchi, Chōshū): Bakumatsu Transformation
evidence.dateBasis: Preserved Edo *bukeyashiki* samurai mud-walls, reverberatory furnace & Yoshida school
evidence.summary: Relegated to Japan Sea margins by the Tokugawa, the Mōri clan's untouched Hagi castle-town built an 1856 Western-style iron reverberatory furnace and nurtured leaders who overturned the Shogunate in 1868.
evidence.limits: Original coastal *tenshu* keep was dismantled peacefully under the 1874 Meiji Castle Edict.

evidence.title: Itchan Kala Walled Inner Town (Khiva, Khwarazm Oasis, Uzbekistan): 17th–19th c. Caravan Seat
evidence.dateBasis: 2.2-km sloped clay-brick ramparts, Juma 213 carved wooden columns & turquoise tiles
evidence.summary: Replacing flood-abandoned Urgench at the end of the Palvan canal, Khiva's mudbrick inner fortress encloses Kunya-Ark, caravanserais, and turquoise-tiled madrasas anchoring Lower Amu Darya trade toward Astrakhan and Orenburg.
evidence.limits: Frequent seismic mudbrick re-plastering renews exterior wall battlements over older cores.

evidence.title: Ipatiev Monastery (Kostroma) & Uglich Kremlin (Upper Volga): 14th–17th c. Timber–Brick Art
evidence.dateBasis: Hypatian Chronicle manuscript heritage & 17th c. frescoed Trinity Cathedral
evidence.summary: Anchoring the upper Volga fur-and-flax navigation corridor north of Moscow, Kostroma's Ipatiev Monastery safeguarded the Hypatian Chronicle while Stroganov and merchant patrons funded luminous painted vaults.
evidence.limits: Soviet Rybinsk–Gorky reservoir dikes altered historic Uglich–Kostroma floodplain contours.

evidence.title: Boyary Rock Art & Minusinsk Okunev Sandstone Steles (Khakassia–Krasnoyarsk): Early Steppe Art
evidence.dateBasis: Engraved solar masks on sandstone megaliths & Afanasievo–Tagar settlement strata
evidence.summary: Basin-ringed Minusinsk meadows preserve solar-horned Okunev stone steles alongside Boyary village-log house petroglyphs depicting Early Iron Age Tagar winter farmsteads.
evidence.limits: Krasnoyarsk Dam inundation flooded lower Yenisei cliff outcrops.

evidence.title: Ado-Tymovo & Imchin Pit-House Villages (Northern Sakhalin): Okhotsk–Nivkh Coastal Trade
evidence.dateBasis: Semi-subterranean whale-and-salmon lodges & Amur iron-silk exchange
evidence.summary: Facing the Tartar Strait across from the Amur mouth, Nivkh and ancient Okhotsk pit-house builders traded Sakhalin sea-mammal oil and sable skins for Jurchen–Qing silk brocades and Chinese iron cauldrons.
evidence.limits: Acidic coastal taiga peat limits deep bone preservation outside shell-bearing pits.

evidence.title: Shujin Brocade Looms & Sanxing–Baidicheng Yangtze–Min River Docks (Sichuan–Chongqing)
evidence.dateBasis: Laoguanshan Han mechanical drawlooms & Tang–Ming Shu river customs
evidence.summary: Laoguanshan tombs in Chengdu preserved multi-shaft pattern looms 1,500 years older than European counterparts, feeding Sichuan brocade down the Yangtze and uphill toward Lhasa and Yunnan.
evidence.limits: Dense modern Chengdu urban development overlies peripheral Han craft wards.

evidence.title: Jinci Maternal Hall & Datong Yungang Frontier Garrison (Shanxi): Northern Wall–Plains Gate
evidence.dateBasis: Northern Song wooden Sage Mother Hall (1038 CE) & Great Wall Datong horse-fair
evidence.summary: Sitting where Fen River farmland meets Shanxi's mountain passes toward Datong's Great Wall horse markets, Jinci preserves Song timber bracket halls alongside cast-iron guardians of 1097 CE.
evidence.limits: Adjacent industrial springs lowered traditional natural artesian headwaters.

evidence.title: Mingzhou / Ningbo Tianyi Pavilion & Tang–Song Shipwreck Hulls (Zhejiang): Maritime Guild Gate
evidence.dateBasis: Excavated Song Yue celadon quays & 1561 Tianyi oldest surviving private library
evidence.summary: Serving as official Tang–Song embassy harbor connecting Hangzhou's Grand Canal terminus to Goryeo Korea, Hakata, and Kamakura Zen temples, Ningbo also guarded East Asia's oldest surviving 1561 private library.
evidence.limits: Estuarine wharf timbers lie deep beneath dense modern port neighborhoods.

evidence.title: Wuxi–Suzhou Grand Canal Docks & Huishan Clay-Figure Guilds (Jiangnan): Textile–Rice Core
evidence.dateBasis: Song–Qing stone bridge quays, silk weaving guilds & Huishan water-transport kilns
evidence.summary: Straddling Taihu Lake along the Jiangnan trunk of the Grand Canal, Wuxi and Suzhou shipped tribute rice, raw white silk, and lacquerware directly north to Beijing and south to Quanzhou.
evidence.limits: 1860s Taiping conflicts destroyed several wooden river warehouses prior to late Qing rebuilds.

evidence.title: Nan'ao No. 1 Ming Wanli Shipwreck & Chaoshan Kiln Littoral (East Guangdong): 1600 CE Sea Route
evidence.dateBasis: 27,000+ intact Zhangzhou–Jingdezhen export porcelains & bronze swivel guns
evidence.summary: Sunk off Shantou with 27,000 stacked Zhangzhou and Jingdezhen bowls, copper coins, and olive pits bound along the Manila–Southeast Asia corridor, Nan'ao No. 1 snapshots peak Wanli maritime exports.
evidence.limits: Sand-shifting currents broke upper timber decking prior to 2010–2012 recovery.

evidence.title: Himeji-jō White Heron Keep (Hyōgo, 1609): Complete Sengoku-Edo Wooden Fortress Network
evidence.dateBasis: 83 original plaster-covered cypress defense rooms, maze alleys & dual sacred pillars
evidence.summary: Unscathed by civil siege or wartime fire since Ikeda Terumasa expanded its keep in 1609, Himeji preserves Japan's most complete maze of lime-plastered *tenshu* ramparts, gunports, and storehouses along the San'yō road.
evidence.limits: Outer third-bailey daimyō residences converted cleanly into civic barracks under Meiji rule.

evidence.title: Shimoda Harbor, Heda Shipbuilding Bay & Nikkō Carpentry Guilds: Late Edo Naval Contact
evidence.dateBasis: 1854 *Heda* Western-rigged schooner carpentry logs & Izu stone quarries
evidence.summary: Quarried first for the monumental ashlar granite ramparts of Edo Castle, the Izu Peninsula's maritime carpenters partnered with shipwrecked Russian sailors in 1854–1855 to build Japan's first Western-rigged schooners at Heda.
evidence.limits: Tsunami surges along Suruga Bay washed away original wooden slipways.

evidence.title: Beypore Traditional Uru Shipyards (Malabar Coast, Kerala): Monsoon Teak Dhows
evidence.dateBasis: Coir-stitched Nilambur teak hulls & Arabic–Malabar navigation tables
evidence.summary: Fed by Nilambur rainforest teak floated down the Chaliyar River, Beypore master *khalasis* craft ocean-going *uru* dhows prized across the Persian Gulf and Red Sea for millennia without modern blueprints.
evidence.limits: Pre-18th-century wooden yards leave minimal surviving dock stonework in shifting estuary mud.

evidence.title: Nagapattinam Chola Bronze Hoard & Kaveripattinam Ports (Tamil Coast): SE Asia Maritime Hub
evidence.dateBasis: Chudamani Srivijaya Vihara grants, 350+ bronze statues & drowned Sangam wharves
evidence.summary: At Nagapattinam, Sailendra kings of Sumatra/Malaya funded an active Srivijayan Buddhist monastery under Chola royal charter (1006 CE), mirroring intense Tamil merchant guild inscriptions in Sumatra and China.
evidence.limits: 2004 tsunami and Holocene coastal erosion reworked early Sangam brick pier remnants.

evidence.title: Panauti–Bhaktapur Brick Canal Towns (Kathmandu Valley, Nepal): 13th–18th c. Newar Guilds
evidence.dateBasis: 1294 CE Indreshwar Mahadev wood-carving & sunken stone *hiti* conduits
evidence.summary: Sustained by trans-Himalayan Lhasa trade and irrigated valley terraces, Newar artisan guilds built multi-tiered brick pagodas, brass shrines, and step-down sunken stone fountains (*hiti*) spanning medieval Nepal.
evidence.limits: Subsurface 1934 and 2015 earthquakes tested unreinforced mud-mortar temple plinths.

evidence.title: Sambas & Singkawang Coastal Goldfields (West Borneo, Indonesia): 8th–19th c. Borneo Ports
evidence.dateBasis: Sambas gold Buddhist–Hindu hoard & West Kalimantan Hakka *kongsi* mines
evidence.summary: Supplying prized alluvial gold, camphor, and Borneo diamonds to Srivijaya and Majapahit before hosting autonomous 18th-century Hakka *kongsi* mining republics, West Kalimantan anchored Borneo's western sea lane.
evidence.limits: Alluvial sluice mining reworked earlier coastal settlement lenses.

evidence.title: Calatagan (Batangas) & Pila Laguna De Bay Cemeteries (Luzon, Philippines): Pre-Spanish Porcelain
evidence.dateBasis: Over 500 pre-colonial graves rich in Sawankhalok, Yuan & Ming export ceramics
evidence.summary: Coastal Batangas and Laguna lake-town communities interred hundreds of Chinese, Thai Sawankhalok, and Vietnamese ceramics alongside inscribed Tagalog ritual pottery centuries before Spanish arrival.
evidence.limits: 1950s–60s commercial pothunting disturbed many peripheral Laguna shoreline cemeteries.

evidence.title: Tamgaly-Tas Ili River Gorge Steles (Almaty, Kazakhstan): 17th c. Oirat–Kalmyk Prayer Cliffs
evidence.dateBasis: Tibetan–Dzungar carved cliff Buddhas & Ili River caravan ferry crossings
evidence.summary: Carved directly onto black river boulders above the main Ili caravan crossing between northern Xinjiang and the Kazakh Steppe, Oirat–Zunghar Tibetan inscriptions record nomadic Buddhist statecraft on Central Asia's threshold.
evidence.limits: No associated permanent stone monastery foundations exist adjacent to the seasonal ferry cliff.

waves.title: Tea Horse Road (Chama Gudao): Pu'er & Lijiang via Chamdo to Lhasa
waves.summary: Mule and human-porter caravans carried compressed Pu'er and Dali tea cakes across the Jinsha, Mekong, and Salween gorges to Lhasa in exchange for Tibetan horses, wool, hides, and medicinal musk.
waves.limits: Seasonal monsoon rockslides cut narrow gorge trails outside paved staging towns.

waves.title: Sichuan Brick-Tea Highway: Chengdu & Ya'an via Kangding & Batang to Lhasa
waves.summary: Sichuan's imperial tea-horse bureaus channeled heavy Ya'an brick tea through Kangding's high border exchange onto Tibetan yak and mule trains ascending across Kham.
waves.limits: Snow-choked 4,500-meter passes closed high sections during midwinter.

waves.title: Trans-Himalayan Gorge Corridors: Lhasa–Shigatse–Mustang–Kathmandu–Ganga Plains
waves.summary: Deep Kali Gandaki, Rasuwa–Kyirong, and Kuti river gorges pierced the Himalayan wall to exchange Tibetan salt, borax, gold, and wool for Nepali silver coins, grain, brassware, and Bengal cotton.
waves.limits: Seasonal glacial-river floodwater alternated with high-pass blizzards.

waves.title: Karakoram & Ladakh High-Pass Route: Srinagar–Leh–Karakoram Pass–Yarkand
waves.summary: Ascending past 5,500 meters across the Karakoram watershed, yak and pony trains linked Kashmir shawls and Indian spices with Changtang pashmina wool, Khotan jade, and Yarkand felt.
waves.limits: High-altitude hypoxia and glaciated passes restricted caravans to brief summer–autumn windows.

waves.title: Bhutan Dzong Passes & Assam–Tibet Corridor: Phari–Paro–Trongsa–Bumthang–Brahmaputra
waves.summary: Guarded by Bhutan's valley *dzong* fortresses, trans-Himalayan trails swapped Tibetan salt and wool for Assamese endi silk, lac dye, rice, and Bengal metalware.
waves.limits: Malaria-prone foothills restricted lower Duar markets to cool winter months.

waves.title: China's Grand Canal (Dayunhe): Hangzhou–Yangzhou–Huai'an–Kaifeng–Beijing Spine
waves.summary: The world's longest engineered inland waterway unified southern rice paddies, Huai salt pans, and Jiangnan silk looms with northern dynastic capitals through summit pound locks.
waves.limits: Repeated Yellow River course shifts disrupted Shandong–Huai'an water levels.

waves.title: Great Wall & Hexi Garrison-Market Arc: Dunhuang–Jiayuguan–Yulin–Beijing–Shanhaiguan
waves.summary: Far more than static ramparts, China's northern Great Wall and Hexi oasis garrisons functioned as a regulated ecological border funneling horse-for-tea markets, soldiers, and Central Asian caravans.
waves.limits: Shifts in Ming–Mongol accords alternated frontier gates between siege warfare and bustling horse fairs.

waves.title: Yangtze & Jingdezhen Porcelain–Tea–Timber Artery: Chongqing–Wuhan–Jingdezhen–Nanjing
waves.summary: Yangtze junk fleets carried Sichuan medicinal timber, Hankou brick tea, and Jingdezhen porcelain barrels out to Grand Canal and East China Sea export warehouses.
waves.limits: Three Gorges rapids required hundreds of human trackers hauling upstream junks past Chongqing.

waves.title: Southwest Silk Road (Shu–Shendu): Chengdu–Dali–Baoshan–Bhamo–Assam–Bengal
waves.summary: Already active when Zhang Qian found Sichuan bamboo staffs and cloth in Bactria in 126 BCE, rugged southwestern valleys connected Shu workshops across northern Myanmar and Assam to Bengal.
waves.limits: Dense malarial valleys and monsoon canyons kept pack tonnage smaller than northwestern oases.

waves.title: East China Sea Porcelain & Silver Arc: Guangzhou–Quanzhou–Zhangzhou–Ryukyu–Nagasaki
waves.summary: Seasonal southwest and northeast monsoons carried Fujian celadons, Zhangzhou porcelains, and raw silk across to Ryukyu and Nagasaki in exchange for Japanese silver, copper, and sulfur.
waves.limits: Late summer typhoons exacted heavy junk losses across the East China Sea.

waves.title: Volga–Baltic–Caspian Silver & Fur Highway: Staraya Ladoga–Novgorod–Bolgar–Astrakhan
waves.summary: Long before railways, Russia's linked river-portage grid pumped northern sable, walrus ivory, honey, and wax down the Volkhov and Volga in exchange for Abbasid/Samanid silver dirhams and Caspian silk.
waves.limits: Winter ice locked northern Volga–Volkhov reaches for nearly five months each year.

waves.title: West Siberian River & Arctic Fur Corridor: Perm–Verkhoturye–Tobolsk–Surgut–Mangazeya
waves.summary: Crossing the Urals via Cherdyn and Verkhoturye onto West Siberia's Ob–Irtysh–Taz rivers, hunters and Pomeranian *kochi* ships extracted tens of thousands of sable pelts through subarctic Mangazeya.
waves.limits: Imperial closure of the Kara Sea route in 1619 rerouted traffic purely onto interior rivers.

waves.title: Trans-Siberian River–Portage Spine: Tomsk–Yeniseysk–Bratsk–Irkutsk–Yakutsk–Okhotsk
waves.summary: Connecting three immense northward-flowing Arctic basins across short wooded portages (Ket–Yenisei, Ilim–Lena, Maya–Judoma), Russian–indigenous boatmen crossed all of northern Asia in under sixty years.
waves.limits: Brief summer ice-free windows forced multiannual wintering along intermediate portage forts.

waves.title: Great Siberian Tea Road: Beijing–Zhangjiakou–Urga–Kiakhta–Irkutsk–Tobolsk–Kazan–Moscow
waves.summary: Established by the 1727 Treaty of Kiakhta, the overland Great Tea Road exchanged Chinese leaf and brick tea, silk, and porcelain for Siberian furs, woolens, and silver via camel caravans and winter sledges.
waves.limits: Competition from Suez Canal steam shipping curtailed long-distance wagon tea volume after 1870.

waves.title: Amur–Kamchatka–Chukotka Pacific Fur Corridor: Irkutsk–Nerchinsk–Albazin–Okhotsk–Avacha
waves.summary: Overland Siberian tea-and-silver wealth financed Pacific shipyards at Okhotsk and Petropavlovsk, linking Evenki, Buryat, Nivkh, Koryak, and Aleutic sea-otter fur exchanges.
waves.limits: Treaty of Nerchinsk (1689) excluded Russian vessels from the lower Amur until 1858.

waves.title: Urals–Irtysh–Altai–Tuva–Baikal Steppe Bronze & Scythian–Pazyryk Corridors
waves.summary: Successive chariot-fort Sintashta, Seima–Turbino tin-bronze casting networks, and mounted Scythian–Arzhan–Pazyryk confederations bound the Southern Urals, Altai, and Lake Baikal across two millennia.
waves.limits: Chronological gaps vary locally across unexcavated forest-steppe tracts.

waves.title: Mongolian Steppe & Örtöö Relay Network: Khovd–Uliastai–Orkhon–Avraga–Urga–Dolonnor
waves.summary: Continuous horse-relay stations (*örtöö*) across Mongolia's grassy valleys knit together Xiongnu bronze–iron founders, Uyghur Manichaean scribes, Chinggisid imperial couriers, and Qing camel tea caravans.
waves.limits: Seasonal nomadic winter camps leave sparser architectural remains than oasis mosques.

waves.title: Korea Strait–Yellow Sea Exchange: Shandong–Gongju–Gyeongju–Gaya–Hakata–Nara
waves.summary: Across the Korea Strait, Gaya iron ingots, Baekje Buddhist artisans, Goryeo celadon, and *Tripitaka* woodblocks flowed steadily from Shandong and Korean harbors to northern Kyushu and Nara.
waves.limits: Storms across the Tsushima narrows sank frequent ceramic freighters such as the 1323 Sinan ship.

waves.title: Tokugawa Five Highways (Gokaidō): Edo–Hakone (Tōkaidō) / Magome (Nakasendō)–Kyoto–Osaka
waves.summary: Gravel-paved postal stations spaced every 8–12 km unified early modern Japan, carrying mandatory *sankin-kōtai* daimyō retinues, courier drafts, pilgrims, and specialty crafts between Edo and the Kansai heartland.
waves.limits: Strict Tokugawa prohibition on wheeled carts meant most overland freight moved by packhorse or porter.

waves.title: Kitamaebune Sea-of-Japan Shipping Arc: Osaka–Seto Inland Sea–Kanazawa–Sakata–Sado–Matsumae
waves.summary: High-prowed *bezaisen* cargo ships pioneered the western circular circuit shipping Matsumae herring fertilizer and kelp from Ezo/Hokkaido down to Osaka indigo, cotton, and rice merchants.
waves.limits: Winter gales off the Japan Sea coast interrupted shipping between November and March.

waves.title: Ryukyu–Red Seal Ship (Shuinsen) Network: Sakai/Nagasaki–Naha–Hội An–Manila–Ayutthaya
waves.summary: Before Tokugawa maritime restrictions in 1635, Ryukyuan royal vessels and shogun-licensed *shuinsen* carried Japanese silver and copper southward for raw silk, deerskins, sappanwood, and Siam ceramics.
waves.limits: Post-1639 Dutch, Chinese, Ryukyu, and Korean channels replaced direct Japanese overseas voyages.

waves.title: Arabian Sea Monsoon Lane: Lothal/Surat–Vadnagar–Konkan–Muziris–Mantai–Galle
waves.summary: Driven by predictable southwest summer and northeast winter monsoon winds, sewn-plank dhows connected Gujarat carnelian/calico workshops and Kerala pepper ports through Sri Lanka's Mantai funnel.
waves.limits: May–August Arabian Sea squalls closed western Indian ports completely during peak monsoon.

waves.title: Maldives Cowrie Money Circuit: Malé–Mantai–Arikamedu–Sonargaon/Chittagong–Yunnan
waves.summary: Ballast sacks of *Cypraea moneta* cowrie shells harvested by Maldivian women circulated as small-change currency in Bengal and overland along the Southwest Silk Road into Yunnan.
waves.limits: Archival shell-tax shipments survive best after 1300 CE.

waves.title: Bay of Bengal–Malacca Monsoon Highway: Bengal/Korkai–Mantai–Bago/Kra Portage–Bujang–Melaka
waves.summary: Combining direct Nicobar–Andaman monsoon crossings and Isthmus of Kra land portages, South Asian textiles, glass beads, and Buddhist–Hindu scripts mingled with Malay tin, camphor, and pepper.
waves.limits: Shifting delta distributaries around Bengal and Pegu relocated historic river anchors inland.

waves.title: Spice Islands Monsoon Highway: Banda–Ternate–Makassar–Majapahit–Palembang–Melaka
waves.summary: Maluku outriggers, Javanese *jong* cargo ships, and Bugis *pinisi* schooners carried endemic cloves from Ternate/Tidore and nutmeg/mace from Banda westward into Java, Sumatra, and world markets.
waves.limits: Pre-1500 indigenous spice voyages appear indirectly in shipwrecks and charred cloves abroad (e.g. Mantai, Terqa).

waves.title: South China Sea Jade, Gold & Ceramic Ring: Taiwan–Batanes–Luzon/Butuan–Kota Batu–Hội An–Quanzhou
waves.summary: Operating first via Taiwan nephrite *lingling-o* ear ornaments and Sa Huỳnh jars, and later via Butuan *balangay* plank boats, Brunei camphor, Champa porcelain, and Quanzhou junks across the South China Sea.
waves.limits: Coral reef shoals across the Spratly–Paracel shelf restricted deep-sea routes to perimeter coasts.

waves.title: Yuan–Mongol Fleets to Korea & Hakata Bay, Japan (1274 & 1281 CE)
waves.summary: Dual Mongol–Yuan–Goryeo fleets launching from Masan and Zhoushan assaulted Tsushima, Iki, and Hakata Bay before stone seawall defense and severe typhoons wrecked the 1281 fleet off Takashima.
waves.limits: Typhoon-scattered seabed hulls span wide muddy sandbanks off Nagasaki Prefecture.

waves.title: Imjin War (1592–1598): Kyushu Staging, Joseon Sieges, Hansando–Myeongnyang & Ming Intervention
waves.summary: Hideyoshi's 1592–1598 invasions mobilized Japanese *sengoku* armies across the Korea Strait while Admiral Yi Sun-sin's coastal squadrons, Korean righteous armies, and Ming relief forces clashed across the peninsula.
waves.limits: War-era wooden Japanese *wajo* and Korean port forts were mostly dismantled after 1598.

waves.title: Muscovite–Cossack Riverine Expansion Across Siberia to the Amur & Kamchatka (1581–1689)
waves.summary: Armed Cossack *druzhinas* and Stroganov river flotillas defeated the Khanate of Sibir (1582), erected riverine *ostrogs* across four Arctic basins, and clashed with Qing forces at Albazin before the 1689 Nerchinsk border.
waves.limits: Resistance by Tatars, Buryats, Evenks, Chukchis, and Koryaks shaped fluid frontier sovereignty.
